math_questions.question: Which situation involves quantities that combine to equal zero?

options.A: receiving $\(8\) as a gift and then giving $\(8\) to a friend
options.B: buying a shirt for $\(12\) and then buying shoes for $\(12\)
options.C: climbing \(4\) flights of stairs, and then climbing \(4\) more flights
options.D: starting \(15\) feet underwater, diving down \(15\) feet, and then diving \(15\) feet more

solution.exhibit_text: Look for two values with the same absolute value where one is positive and one is negative. Receiving a $\(8\) gift is \(+8\), and giving away $\(8\) is \(-8\). These combine to zero: \(+8-8=0\).

base_question.question: Which situation involves quantities that combine to equal zero?

options.A: receiving $\(5\) as a gift and then giving $\(5\) to a friend
options.B: buying a book for $\(10\) and then buying lunch for $\(10\)
options.C: getting on an elevator at the ground floor, rising \(3\) floors, and then rising \(3\) more floors
options.D: starting in a cave \(20\) feet below the ground, climbing up \(20\) feet, and then climbing up \(20\) feet more

solution.exhibit_text:
(A) When looking for a situation where quantities combine to make zero, find two values with the same absolute value where one value is positive and one value is negative.

In the situation in option A, receiving a gift of $\(5\) is represented by \(+5\), and giving a friend $\(5\) is represented by \(-5\). These values combine to equal zero because \(+5 - 5 = 0\).

math_questions.question: \[Q=\dfrac{R}{5}=S-4=8T=\dfrac{U}{6}>0\]\nAccording to the statement above, which variable has the **least** value?

solution.exhibit_text: Pick a simple value for \(Q\), like \(2\). Then \(R=5(2)=10\); \(S=2+4=6\); \(T=\dfrac{2}{8}=0.25\); \(U=6(2)=12\). Comparing \(10, 6, 0.25, 12\), the smallest is \(T\).

base_question.question:
\[Q=\dfrac{R}{3}=S-6=7T=\dfrac{U}{10}>0\]
According to the statement above, which variable has the **least** value?

solution.exhibit_text:
Because it's easiest to compare these quantities if you have numbers instead of variables, pick a simple number to substitute for \(Q\), like 2. Take each piece of the equation at a time and solve for each of the answer choices:

\[Q=\dfrac{R}{3} \Rightarrow 2=\dfrac{R}{3} \Rightarrow R=6\]
\[Q=S-6 \Rightarrow 2=S-6 \Rightarrow S=8\]
\[Q=7T \Rightarrow 2=7T \Rightarrow T=\dfrac{2}{7}\]
\[Q=\dfrac{U}{10} \Rightarrow 2=\dfrac{U}{10} \Rightarrow U=20\]

The only fraction and thus the smallest number is \(T\).

math_questions.question: \(P\) is the center of the circle shown above. \(\overline{AB}\) is a diameter. The perimeter of rectangle \(ABCD\) is \(90\) cm. \(\overline{PQ}\) is a radius, and \(Q\) is on \(\overline{CD}\). What is the circumference of the circle?

solution.exhibit_text: Let the short side of the rectangle (equal to the radius) be \(x\) and the long side (the diameter) be \(2x\). The perimeter is \(x+x+2x+2x=6x=90\), so \(x=15\). The radius is \(15\) cm, so the circumference is \(2\pi(15)=30\pi\).

base_question.question: \(P\) is the center of the circle shown above. \(\overline{AB}\) is a diameter. The perimeter of rectangle \(ABCD\) is \(72\) cm. \(\overline{PQ}\) is a radius, and \(Q\) is on \(\overline{CD}\). What is the circumference of the circle?

solution.exhibit_text:
From the information given, you know that \(\overline{AB}\) is one side of the rectangle and also the diameter of the circle. You also know that \(\overline{PQ}\) is the radius of the circle and equal to \(\overline{AD}\), which is another side of the rectangle.

Since the diameter is twice the radius, you can designate the short and long sides of the rectangle as \(x\) and \(2x\), respectively. Find the perimeter of the rectangle by adding up all the sides:

\[72\text{ cm}=x+x+2x+2x\]
\[72\text{ cm}=6x\]
\[12\text{ cm}=x\]

The radius of the circle is thus \(12\) cm. Therefore, the circumference \(=2\pi r=2\pi(12)=24\pi\).

math_questions.question: A student is choosing \(4\) books to read over the summer from a list of \(8\) different recommended novels. How many different sets of \(4\) books can the student choose?

solution.exhibit_text: There are \(8\times7\times6\times5=1{,}680\) ways to choose \(4\) books in order. Since order doesn't matter, divide by the number of ways to arrange \(4\) books, \(4\times3\times2\times1=24\): \(\dfrac{1{,}680}{24}=70\).

base_question.question: A student is choosing 3 books to read over the summer from a list of 7 different recommended novels. How many different sets of 3 books can the student choose?

solution.exhibit_text:
The student must choose 3 books to read. Since there are 7 available books, there are 7 options for the first book. After the first book has been selected, there are only 6 left to choose from. Similarly, after the second has been selected, there are only 5 left. Therefore, there are \(7\times6\times5=210\) total ways to choose the three books.

However, this method imposes an order on the way the books are chosen. In reality, choosing 3 books from a group of 7 can be done in any order you want. To account for this, you must divide by the total number of ways to arrange 3 books, which is \(3\times2\times1=6\). Therefore, the final result is \(\dfrac{210}{6}=35\).

math_questions.question: Over a one-month period, a software team is assigned a total of \(200\) tasks for a new application. The table above shows the first three phases of tasks within the larger project. What percentage of the \(200\) tasks is the **total** number of tasks in these first three phases?

solution.exhibit_text: Because the ranges are inclusive, use End \(-\) Start \(+1\). Phase I: \((10-1)+1=10\). Phase II: \((33-20)+1=14\). Phase III: \((60-45)+1=16\). Total: \(10+14+16=40\). Percentage: \(\dfrac{40}{200}\times100\%=20.0\%\).

base_question.question: Over a one-month period, a software team is assigned a total of 250 tasks for a new application. The table above shows the first three phases of tasks within the larger project. What percentage of the 250 tasks is the **total** number of tasks in these first three phases?

solution.exhibit_text:
To find the percentage, you must first calculate the total number of tasks in the three phases and then divide by the total project size. Because the ranges are inclusive, use the formula End − Start + 1.

Phase I: \((12-1)+1=12\)
Phase II: \((34-20)+1=15\)
Phase III: \((60-42)+1=19\)

Thus, the total number of tasks for these three phases is \(12+15+19=46\). Use \(\text{Percent}=\dfrac{\text{Part}}{\text{Whole}}\times 100\%\) to calculate the percentage:

\[\dfrac{46}{250}\times 100\% = \dfrac{46}{250}\times\dfrac{4}{4}\times 100\%\]
\[=\dfrac{184}{1{,}000}\times 100\%\]
\[=\dfrac{184}{10}\%\]
\[=18.4\%\]

math_questions.question: Suppose \(R=\dfrac{a}{b}\) and \(S=\dfrac{a+3}{b+3}\), and \(a\) and \(b\) do not equal \(-3\) or \(0\). What is \(\dfrac{R}{S}\) in terms of \(a\) and \(b\)?

solution.exhibit_text: \(\dfrac{R}{S}=\dfrac{a}{b}\div\dfrac{a+3}{b+3}=\dfrac{a}{b}\times\dfrac{b+3}{a+3}=\dfrac{a(b+3)}{b(a+3)}\). Distributing gives \(\dfrac{ab+3a}{ab+3b}\).

base_question.question: Suppose \(R=\dfrac{a}{b}\) and \(S=\dfrac{a+1}{b+1}\), and \(a\) and \(b\) do not equal \(-1\) or \(0\). What is \(\dfrac{R}{S}\) in terms of \(a\) and \(b\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
Substitute the values of \(R\) and \(S\) into the fraction \(\dfrac{R}{S}\) and simplify:

\[\dfrac{R}{S}=\dfrac{\tfrac{a}{b}}{\tfrac{a+1}{b+1}}\]
\[=\dfrac{a}{b}\div\dfrac{a+1}{b+1}\]
\[=\dfrac{a}{b}\times\dfrac{b+1}{a+1}\]
\[=\dfrac{a(b+1)}{b(a+1)}\]

Distribute \(a\) and \(b\) to get \(\dfrac{ab+a}{ab+b}\).

math_questions.question: The table shows the cups of ingredients used to make \(4\) servings of snack mix. What is the unit rate for cups of pretzels per cup of cereal?

solution.exhibit_text: Divide cups of pretzels by cups of cereal: \(\dfrac{2/3}{1\tfrac{3}{4}}=\dfrac{2}{3}\div\dfrac{7}{4}=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{4}{7}=\dfrac{8}{21}\).

base_question.question: The table shows the cups of ingredients used to make \(5\) servings of trail mix. What is the unit rate for cups of peanuts per cup of raisins?

solution.exhibit_text:
The word "per" means "divide." To find the unit rate for cups of peanuts per cup of raisins, divide the amount of peanuts by the amount of raisins:

\[\dfrac{\text{cups of peanuts}}{\text{cups of raisins}}=\dfrac{\frac{3}{4}}{2\frac{1}{2}}\]

First, convert the mixed number \(2\dfrac{1}{2}\) into an improper fraction: \(2\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{5}{2}\).

Next, divide the fractions. To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal:

\[\dfrac{\text{cups of peanuts}}{\text{cups of raisins}}=\dfrac{3}{4}\div\dfrac{5}{2}=\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{2}{5}=\dfrac{6}{20}=\dfrac{3}{10}\]

math_questions.question: A debate committee must be formed, consisting of exactly \(1\) captain and \(2\) members. If there are \(5\) possible captains and \(7\) possible members available to join the committee, how many different ways are there to form the committee?

solution.exhibit_text: There are \(5\) choices for captain. For the \(2\) members from \(7\) people, there are \(\dfrac{7\times6}{2}=21\) ways (dividing by \(2\) since order doesn't matter). Multiply: \(5\times21=105\).

base_question.question: A school debate committee must be formed, consisting of exactly 1 teacher and 2 students. If there are 4 teachers and 6 students available to join the committee, how many different ways are there to form the committee?

solution.exhibit_text: The committee contains exactly 1 teacher. There are 4 possible teachers to choose from, so there are 4 options for this position. The remaining 2 positions must be filled from the 6 available students. There are thus 6 choices for one position. Once this person is assigned, there are only 5 left to choose from. This appears to yield \(6\times5=30\) options for the students. However, this method counts Student A and Student B as a different group than Student B and Student A. In reality, they should be the same because order does not matter in a committee. To correct for this, divide 30 by the number of different ways of arranging 2 students, which is 2. This yields \(30\div2=15\) groups of 2 students. Multiply this by the number of options for the teacher to arrive at the total number of ways of selecting the committee: \(4\times15=60\).

math_questions.question: In the right triangle shown above, what is the measure of the smallest angle?

options.C: \(46\degree\)

solution.exhibit_text: Since the two non-right angles sum to \(90\degree\): \((3x-5)+(2x+10)=90\), so \(5x+5=90\), \(5x=85\), \(x=17\). The angles are \(3(17)-5=46\degree\) and \(2(17)+10=44\degree\). The smallest is \(44\degree\).

base_question.question: In the right triangle shown above, what is the measure of the smallest angle?

solution.exhibit_text:
(A) Since the three angles of a triangle have a sum of \(180°\), and since one angle is a right angle, the other two angles have a sum of \(90°\). By writing an equation and using inverse operations, the value of \(x\) can be found.

\[(2x + 9) + (3x - 14) = 90\]
\[5x - 5 = 90\]
\[5x = 95\]
\[x = 19\]

Now, use substitution to find the measure of the two angles to determine the smallest angle of the triangle.

\[2x + 9 = 2(19) + 9 = 47\]
\[3x - 14 = 3(19) - 14 = 43\]

math_questions.question: For each \(\dfrac{2}{5}\) foot of ribbon trim, \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) yard of lace is needed. How many yards of lace are needed per foot of ribbon trim?

solution.exhibit_text: It takes \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) yard of lace for \(\dfrac{2}{5}\) foot of trim. To find the amount for \(1\) foot, divide: \(1 \div \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{5}{2}\). So the amount needed per foot is \(\dfrac{5}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{15}{8}\) yd.

base_question.question: For each \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) foot of curtain width, \(\dfrac{5}{6}\) yard of fabric is needed to make ruffles. How many yards of fabric are needed per foot of curtain width?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) It takes \(\dfrac{5}{6}\) yard of fabric to make \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) foot of curtain width.

To find the ratio of \(1\) foot of curtain width to \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) foot of curtain width \(\left(1{:}\dfrac{3}{8}\right)\), divide.

\[1 \div \dfrac{3}{8} = 1 \times \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3}\]

So the amount of fabric needed for \(1\) foot of curtain width is \(\dfrac{8}{3}\) times the amount needed for \(\dfrac{3}{8}\) foot of curtain width.

\[\dfrac{8}{3} \times \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{40}{18}\]
\[\dfrac{40 \div 2}{18 \div 2} = \dfrac{20}{9}\]

The amount of fabric needed for \(1\) foot of curtain width is \(\dfrac{20}{9}\) yd.

math_questions.question: A coin jar contains quarters, dimes, and nickels. If the ratio of quarters to dimes is \(3{:}5\) and the ratio of quarters to nickels is \(2{:}7\), what is the ratio of dimes to nickels?

solution.exhibit_text: To combine the ratios, make the quarters-number match. Multiply the first ratio (quarters to dimes) by \(2\): \(6:10\). Multiply the second ratio (quarters to nickels) by \(3\): \(6:21\). Now that quarters match (\(6\)), the ratio of dimes to nickels is \(10:21\).

base_question.question: The spare change on a dresser is composed of pennies, nickels, and dimes. If the ratio of pennies to nickels is 2:3 and the ratio of pennies to dimes is 3:4, what is the ratio of nickels to dimes?

solution.exhibit_text: Don't fall into the "obvious answer" trap of just taking the numbers of nickels and dimes from the two ratios to come up with 3:4. To find the ratio of nickels to dimes, you need to get the two ratios in proportion to one another by getting the same number of pennies in each. Multiplying the first ratio (pennies to nickels) by 3 gives you 6:9; multiplying the second ratio (pennies to dimes) by 2 gives you 6:8. Since the number corresponding to pennies is now the same in each ratio (6), the ratio of nickels to dimes can now be found. The ratio of nickels to dimes is 9:8.

math_questions.question: Rosa started her summer job making $\(15\) an hour. After a few weeks, her wages increased by \(10\%\). Later, she received an additional \(25\%\) increase. What was the total percentage increase in wages that Rosa received?

solution.exhibit_text: First increase: \(15\times1.10=16.50\). Second increase: \(16.50\times1.25=20.625\). Percent change: \(\dfrac{20.625-15}{15}\times100\%=37.5\%\).

base_question.question: Sally started her summer job making $12 an hour. After three weeks, her wages increased by 20%. Two weeks later, she received an additional 15% increase. What was the total percentage increase in wages that Sally received?

solution.exhibit_text:
The formula for calculating percent increase is \(\text{Percent Change}=\dfrac{\text{Change}}{\text{Original}}\times100\%\). The question gives you the original amount ($12), but you need to calculate Sally's final wage before you can use the formula.

Her first increase was by 20%: \(\$12\times1.20=\$12(1+0.20)=\$12+\$2.40=\$14.40\). The final increase was by 15%, so:

\[\$14.40\times1.15=\$14.40(1+0.10+0.05)\]
\[=\$14.40+\$1.44+\$0.72\]
\[=\$16.56\]

(Note: adding a 1 before the percentage includes the original whole in the new total wage and saves you the need to add the increase to the original amount.)

Next, put the starting and ending wages into the percent change formula:

\[\text{Percent Change}=\dfrac{16.56-12}{12}\times100\%\]
\[=\dfrac{4.56}{12}\times100\%\]
\[=38\%\]

math_questions.question: On the number line above, points \(W\), \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) are integers, and \(WX{:}XY{:}YZ = 5{:}3{:}2\). What is the value of \(\overline{WY}\)?

solution.exhibit_text: \(WY\) covers the \(WX\) and \(XY\) portions, which together are \(\dfrac{5+3}{5+3+2}=\dfrac{8}{10}=\dfrac{4}{5}\) of \(WZ\). Since \(W=-6\) and \(Z=24\), \(WZ=24-(-6)=30\). So \(WY=\dfrac{4}{5}(30)=24\).

base_question.question: On the number line above, points \(W\), \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) are integers, and \(WX{:}XY{:}YZ = 4{:}2{:}3\). What is the value of \(\overline{WY}\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) Convert the ratios into fractions of \(WZ\). Use the sum of the ratios for the denominator.

\[WX{:}XY{:}YZ = 4{:}2{:}3\]
\[WX = \dfrac{4}{4+2+3} = \dfrac{4}{9}\]
\[XY = \dfrac{2}{4+2+3} = \dfrac{2}{9}\]

The part of \(WZ\) that is \(WY\) is the sum of those fractions:

\[WY = \dfrac{4}{9} + \dfrac{2}{9} = \dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}\]

Find the length of \(WZ\):

\[WZ = 8 - (-10) = 18\]

The value of \(WY\) is \(\dfrac{2}{3}(18) = 12\).

math_questions.question: A person buys a used truck with a down payment of $\(1{,}500\) and makes monthly payments of $\(310\) for \(4\) years. What is the total amount the person pays for the truck?

solution.exhibit_text: There are \(12 \times 4 = 48\) months. Total monthly payments: \(310 \times 48 = 14{,}880\). Total cost: \(14{,}880 + 1{,}500 = 16{,}380\).

base_question.question: A person buys a used car with a down payment of $\(1{,}200\) and makes monthly payments of $\(275\) for \(3\) years. What is the total amount the person pays for the car?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) Determine the total cost of the car by adding the down payment to the total monthly payments over \(3\) years.

There are \(12\) months in a year, so multiply (\(12\) months/year \(\times\) \(3\) years) to get a total of \(36\) months. Determine the total monthly payments by multiplying the monthly payment (\$\(275\)) \(\times\) the total number of months (\(36\)):

\[275 \times 36 = 9{,}900\]

Determine the total cost of the car by adding the down payment (\$\(1{,}200\)) to the total monthly payments (\$\(9{,}900\)):

\[9{,}900 + 1{,}200 = 11{,}100\]

The total cost of the car is \$\(11{,}100\).

math_questions.question: Today, Maya's age is \(\dfrac{1}{5}\) of Liam's age. In \(3\) years, Maya's age will be \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) of Liam's age. How old is Liam today?

options.C: \(40\) years old

solution.exhibit_text: Let Maya's age be \(M\) and Liam's age be \(L\). Today: \(M = \dfrac{1}{5}L\). In 3 years: \(M + 3 = \dfrac{1}{4}(L+3)\). Substitute: \(\dfrac{1}{5}L + 3 = \dfrac{1}{4}(L+3)\). Multiply both sides by 20: \(4L + 60 = 5(L+3) = 5L + 15\). So \(60 - 15 = 5L - 4L\), giving \(L = 45\).

base_question.question: Today, Tien's age is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) of Jordan's age. In \(2\) years, Tien's age will be \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) of Jordan's age. How old is Jordan today?

options.C: \(12\) years old

solution.exhibit_text:
(D) Set up an equation to express Tien's age (\(T\)) and Jordan's age (\(J\)) today:

\[T = \dfrac{1}{4}J\]

Two years from now, Tien's age will be \(T + 2\) and Jordan's age will be \(J + 2\). Set up an equation about the relationship between Tien's age and Jordan's age in two years:

\[T + 2 = \dfrac{1}{3}(J + 2)\]

Solve the above equation for \(T\):

\[T = \dfrac{1}{3}(J + 2) - 2\]

Now set the two equations equal to each other and solve for \(J\):

\[\dfrac{1}{4}J = \dfrac{1}{3}(J + 2) - 2\]
\[\dfrac{1}{4}J = \dfrac{1}{3}J - \dfrac{4}{3}\]

Multiply both sides by \(12\) to clear fractions and solve for \(J\):

\[3J = 4J - 16\]
\[J = 16\]

math_questions.question: A flat circular metal washer has an outer radius of \(11\) millimeters. The circular hole in the center of the washer has a circumference of \(8\pi\) millimeters. What is the area of the metal face of the washer?

options.C: \(105\pi\) sq mm

solution.exhibit_text: The area of the metal face is the outer disc's area minus the hole's area. Outer disc: \(\pi(11)^2=121\pi\) sq mm. The hole's circumference is \(8\pi\), so \(2\pi r=8\pi\) gives \(r=4\); the hole's area is \(\pi(4)^2=16\pi\) sq mm. The metal face area is \(121\pi-16\pi=105\pi\) sq mm.

base_question.question: A flat circular metal washer has an outer radius of 9 millimeters. The circular hole in the center of the washer has a circumference of \(6\pi\) millimeters. What is the area of the metal face of the washer?

options.C: \(45\pi\) sq mm

solution.exhibit_text: The area of the metal face of the washer is the area of the circular metal disc minus the area of the circular hole. The formula for the area of a circle is \(\pi r^2\). Since the outer radius is 9 mm, the area of the disc is \(\pi(9^2)=81\pi\) sq mm. To calculate the area of the circular hole, find the radius from the given circumference. The formula for circumference is \(2\pi r\). Since the circumference of the circular hole is \(6\pi\) mm, \(2\pi r=6\pi\) and \(r=3\) mm. Thus, the area of the circular hole is \(\pi(3^2)\) sq mm. Putting everything together, the area of the metal face of the washer is \(81\pi-9\pi=72\pi\) sq mm.

math_questions.question: The distance a cyclist travels is proportional to the time spent cycling. A cyclist travels \(108\) miles in \(4\) hours. What is the constant of proportionality for this relationship?

solution.exhibit_text: The constant of proportionality is the ratio of distance to time: \(108 \div 4 = 27\).

base_question.question: The distance an eagle flies is proportional to the time the eagle spends flying. An eagle flies \(90\) miles in \(3\) hours. What is the constant of proportionality for this relationship?

solution.exhibit_text: (B) The constant of proportionality is the ratio of \(y\) (\(90\)) to \(x\) (\(3\)). \(90 \div 3 = 30\). So the constant of proportionality is \(30\).

math_questions.question: In a scale drawing of a triangular banner, one side measures \(18\) centimeters and the other two sides each measure \(14\) centimeters. On the actual banner, these two sides each measure \(42\) feet. What is the length of the remaining side of the actual banner?

solution.exhibit_text: Let \(x\) be the remaining side of the actual banner. Set up a proportion: \(\dfrac{x}{18} = \dfrac{42}{14}\). Solve: \(x = 18 \times 3 = 54\) ft.

base_question.question: In a scale drawing of a triangular banner, one side measures \(16\) centimeters and the other two sides each measure \(12\) centimeters. On the actual banner, these two sides each measure \(36\) feet. What is the length of the remaining side of the actual banner?

solution.exhibit_text:
(D) Let \(x\) be the remaining side of the actual banner.

Set up a proportion:

\[\dfrac{x}{16} = \dfrac{36}{12}\]
\[x = 48 \text{ ft}\]

math_questions.question: On parallelogram \(PQRS\) above, the length of \(\overline{QT}\) is \(20\) centimeters and the length of \(\overline{PS}\) is \(28\) centimeters. What is the area of the parallelogram?

solution.exhibit_text: \(\overline{PS}\) is a base of the parallelogram (\(28\) cm) and \(\overline{QT}\) is the height (\(20\) cm). Area \(=\) base \(\times\) height \(= 28\times20=560\) sq cm.

base_question.question: On parallelogram \(PQRS\) above, the length of \(\overline{QT}\) is \(18\) centimeters. What is the area of the parallelogram?

\[34 \text{ cm} \times 18 \text{ cm} = 612 \text{ cm}^2\]

solution.exhibit_text: The distance from \(M\) to \(T\) is \(\dfrac{2}{3}-\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=1\). Divided into \(5\) equal sections, each section is \(\dfrac{1}{5}\). \(R\) is \(2\) sections from \(M\): \(-\dfrac{1}{3}+2\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)=-\dfrac{5}{15}+\dfrac{6}{15}=\dfrac{1}{15}\).

base_question.question: The hash marks on the number line above are evenly spaced. What is the coordinate of point \(R\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) There are \(5\) sections between \(M\) and \(T\). To find the length of one of these sections, find the distance between \(M\) and \(T\) and divide by \(5\):

\[\left(\dfrac{5}{8} - \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\right) \div \dfrac{5}{1} =\]
\[\left(\dfrac{5}{8} + \dfrac{2}{8}\right) \div \dfrac{5}{1} =\]
\[\dfrac{7}{8} \div \dfrac{5}{1} = \dfrac{7}{8} \times \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{7}{40}\]

\(R\) is \(3\) sections away from \(M\), so add:

\[-\dfrac{1}{4} + 3\left(\dfrac{7}{40}\right) = -\dfrac{10}{40} + \dfrac{21}{40} = \dfrac{11}{40}\]

\(R\) is located at \(\dfrac{11}{40}\).

math_questions.question: The perimeter of square \(A\) is five times the perimeter of an equilateral triangle \(B\). What is the ratio of the length of one side of square \(A\) to the length of one side of equilateral triangle \(B\)?

solution.exhibit_text: Let the square's side be \(s_A\) and the triangle's side be \(s_B\). The perimeter of the square is \(4s_A\), and the perimeter of the triangle is \(3s_B\). \"The perimeter of the square is five times the perimeter of the triangle\" gives \(4s_A=5(3s_B)=15s_B\). Dividing both sides by \(4s_B\): \(\dfrac{s_A}{s_B}=\dfrac{15}{4}\).

base_question.question: The perimeter of a square A is three times the perimeter of an equilateral triangle B. What is the ratio of the length of one side of square A to the length of one side of equilateral triangle B?

solution.exhibit_text:
To find the ratio of the side lengths, set up an algebraic relationship based on the perimeters. The perimeter of a square with side \(s_A\) is \(4s_A\), and the perimeter of an equilateral triangle with side \(s_B\) is \(3s_B\). Translating "the perimeter of the square is three times the perimeter of the triangle" into math gives \(4s_A = 3(3s_B)\), which simplifies to \(4s_A = 9s_B\). Obtain the ratio of the side lengths \(\dfrac{s_A}{s_B}\) by dividing both sides by 4 and then by \(s_B\):

\[\dfrac{s_A}{s_B} = \dfrac{9s_B}{4} \Big/ s_B\]
\[\dfrac{s_A}{s_B} = \dfrac{9}{4}\]

math_questions.question: A jar contains \(96\) buttons that are black, white, or gray. The ratio of black to white buttons is \(9{:}4\), and the ratio of white to gray buttons is \(4{:}3\). If \(3\) white buttons are removed and replaced with \(3\) gray buttons, what will be the new ratio of black to gray buttons?

solution.exhibit_text: The ratio of black to white to gray is \(9{:}4{:}3\) (white matches in both given ratios, so they chain directly). The sum is \(16\), and \(96 \div 16 = 6\) per part, so black \(=54\), white \(=24\), gray \(=18\). After removing \(3\) white and adding \(3\) gray: white \(=21\), gray \(=21\). Black is unchanged at \(54\). The new ratio of black to gray is \(54{:}21\), which simplifies to \(18{:}7\).

base_question.question: A bag contains \(75\) marbles that are red, blue, or green. The ratio of red to blue marbles is \(15{:}7\), and the ratio of blue to green marbles is \(7{:}3\). If \(2\) blue marbles are removed and replaced with \(2\) green marbles, what will be the new ratio of red to green marbles?

solution.exhibit_text:
(D) The ratio of red to blue to green is \(15{:}7{:}3\). Find the proportion of blue marbles: add the numbers of the ratio and use the total sum as the denominator: \(\dfrac{7}{15+7+3} = \dfrac{7}{25}\). The proportion of green marbles is \(\dfrac{3}{25}\).

Since there are \(75\) marbles total, the number of blue marbles is \(\dfrac{7}{25} \times 75 = 21\). The number of green marbles is \(\dfrac{3}{25} \times 75 = 9\).

The number of red marbles is \(75 - 21 - 9 = 45\). If \(2\) blue marbles are removed and replaced with \(2\) green marbles, the number of blue marbles will be \(19\) and the number of green marbles will be \(11\). The ratio of red to green will be \(45{:}11\).

math_questions.question: A box contains \(7\) blue index cards, \(4\) yellow index cards, and \(5\) green index cards. If a student pulls out \(2\) cards at random from this box, without replacement, what is the probability that both cards are **not** green?

solution.exhibit_text: There are \(16\) cards total, and \(11\) are not green. The probability the first card is not green is \(\dfrac{11}{16}\). After removing one, there are \(15\) cards left, \(10\) not green, so the probability is \(\dfrac{10}{15}\). Multiply: \(\dfrac{11}{16}\times\dfrac{10}{15}=\dfrac{110}{240}=\dfrac{11}{24}\).

base_question.question: A box contains \(6\) red index cards, \(3\) yellow index cards, and \(4\) green index cards. If Gabriella pulls out \(2\) cards at random from this box, without replacement, what is the probability that both cards are **not** green?

solution.exhibit_text: Remember that "without replacement" means Gabriella will not put the first card she drew back before she pulls out a second one, so the probabilities will be different for each draw. At first, there are \(13\) index cards, and \(9\) are not green. After one card is drawn, there are \(12\) cards, and \(8\) are not green. You need to multiply to find the probability of both events occurring: \(\dfrac{9}{13}\times\dfrac{8}{12}\). Cross canceling simplifies this to \(\dfrac{3}{13}\times\dfrac{2}{1}=\dfrac{6}{13}\).

math_questions.question: The figure above shows a triangle inscribed in a rectangle. The base of the triangle has a length of \(3\) centimeters, and the rectangle measures \(12\) centimeters by \(15\) centimeters. What is the ratio of the shaded part of the figure to the unshaded part?

solution.exhibit_text: The rectangle's area is \(12\times15=180\) sq cm. The triangle (unshaded) has base \(3\) and height \(15\) (the rectangle's side), so its area is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(3)(15)=22.5\) sq cm. The shaded area is \(180-22.5=157.5\) sq cm. The ratio of shaded to unshaded is \(157.5:22.5\), which simplifies to \(7:1\).

base_question.question: The figure above shows a triangle inscribed in a rectangle. The base of the triangle has a length of 2 centimeters. What is the ratio of the shaded part of the figure to the unshaded part?

solution.exhibit_text:
First, find the area of the rectangle, in square centimeters, using the formula \(A=\ell\times w\): \(A=14\times10=140\) square cm.

Next, find the area of the triangle using the formula \(A=\tfrac{1}{2}bh\). This is the unshaded part of the figure. Notice that the height of the triangle is the same as the side length of the rectangle, 14 cm.

\[A=\tfrac{1}{2}bh\]
\[=\tfrac{1}{2}(2)(14)\]
\[=1(14)=14\]

To find the area of the shaded part of the figure, subtract the area of the triangle from the area of the rectangle to arrive at \(140-14=126\) square centimeters. Thus, the ratio of the shaded part of the figure to the unshaded part is 126:14, which simplifies to 9:1.

math_questions.question:
Two sets, \(R\) and \(S\), are described below. The sum of the elements in set \(R\) equals the sum of the elements in set \(S\).

\[R = \{7, x, 2, 9\}\]
\[S = \{5, y, 3, 6\}\]

What is the value of \(x - y\)?

solution.exhibit_text: The sum for set \(R\) is \(7+x+2+9=x+18\). The sum for set \(S\) is \(5+y+3+6=y+14\). Setting these equal: \(x+18=y+14\), so \(x=y-4\), and \(x-y=-4\).

base_question.question:
Two sets, \(R\) and \(S\), are described below. The sum of the elements in set \(R\) equals the sum of the elements in set \(S\).

\[R = \{5, x, 3, 8\}\]
\[S = \{6, y, 4, 1\}\]

What is the value of \(x - y\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
(B) First, find the sum for each set by adding the terms in each set separately.

The sum for set \(R\) is \(5 + x + 3 + 8\), which is \(x + 16\).

The sum for set \(S\) is \(6 + y + 4 + 1\), which is \(y + 11\).

The question states that these two sums are equal to each other, so write the equation and then rearrange using inverse operations.

\[x + 16 = y + 11\]
\[x = y - 5\]
\[x - y = -5\]

math_questions.question: What is the prime factorization of \(4{,}725\)?

solution.exhibit_text: \(4{,}725 \div 25 = 189\), so \(25 = 5^2\) is a factor. \(189 = 27 \times 7 = 3^3 \times 7\). The prime factorization is \(5^2 \times 3^3 \times 7\).

base_question.question: What is the prime factorization of \(3{,}575\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
(B) By observation, \(3{,}575\) ends in \(75\); therefore, \(3{,}575\) is divisible by \(25\).

\[3{,}575 \div 25 = 143\]

Test \(143\) for factors and eliminate \(3\), \(5\), and \(7\), but \(11\) is a factor.

\[143 \div 11 = 13\text{; both } 11 \text{ and } 13 \text{ are prime numbers.}\]

The first factor, \(25\), is **not** prime but is the product of primes, \(5 \times 5 = 5^2\).

The prime factorization of \(3{,}575\) is \(5^2 \times 11 \times 13\).

math_questions.question: A delivery company uses the formula \(T=\dfrac{d}{r}+s\) to calculate the total delivery time, \(T\), for a package. In this formula, \(d\) represents the distance in miles, \(r\) is a constant representing the average speed, and \(s\) is a fixed setup time. If the company wants to determine the distance based on the total time, which of the following represents the formula solved for \(d\)?

options.C: \(d=\dfrac{T-s}{r}\)

solution.exhibit_text: Subtract \(s\) from both sides: \(T-s=\dfrac{d}{r}\). Multiply both sides by \(r\): \(r(T-s)=d\).

base_question.question: A shipping company uses the formula \(C=\dfrac{w}{k}+b\) to calculate the total shipping cost, \(C\), for a package. In this formula, \(w\) represents the weight of the package in pounds, \(k\) is a constant representing the weight-to-shipping-rate ratio, and \(b\) is a fixed handling fee. If the company wants to determine the weight of a package based on the total cost, which of the following represents the formula solved for \(w\)?

options.C: \(w=\dfrac{C-b}{k}\)

solution.exhibit_text: To solve this question, rearrange the equation so that \(w\) is alone on one side and everything else is on the other. Begin by subtracting \(b\) from both sides to obtain \(C-b=\dfrac{w}{k}\). Now multiply both sides by \(k\) to clear the fraction: \(k(C-b)=w\).

math_questions.question: Which inequality describes the solution set for \(3x - 1 \le y \le 5x + 8\) when \(y = 4\)?

options.C: \(\dfrac{4}{5} \le x \le \dfrac{5}{3}\)

solution.exhibit_text: Split into two inequalities and substitute \(y=4\). From \(3x-1\le4\): \(3x\le5\), so \(x\le\dfrac{5}{3}\). From \(4\le5x+8\): \(-4\le5x\), so \(x\ge-\dfrac{4}{5}\). The solution is \(-\dfrac{4}{5}\le x\le\dfrac{5}{3}\).

base_question.question: Which number line below shows the solution set for \(2x - 2 \le y \le 4x + 10\) when \(y = 1\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) Separate the compound inequality into two pieces:

\[2x - 2 \le y \text{ and } y \le 4x + 10\]

Substitute \(y = 1\) into each inequality and solve for \(x\):

\[2x - 2 \le 1\]
\[2x \le 3\]
\[x \le \dfrac{3}{2}\]

\[1 \le 4x + 10\]
\[-9 \le 4x\]
\[-\dfrac{9}{4} \le x\]

The solution is the number line that shows that \(x\) is greater than or equal to \(-2\tfrac{1}{4}\) and less than or equal to \(1\tfrac{1}{2}\).

base_question.question: A store manager purchases a piece of furniture for $\(456.00\). To determine the selling price, the manager increases the purchase cost by \(125\%\). A customer buys the furniture and pays an additional \(8\%\) sales tax. How much does the customer pay for the furniture?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) Given a purchase price of $\(456.00\), the \(125\%\) increase in price is calculated as:

\[456 \times 1.25 = 570\]

The selling price equals the purchase price plus the increase, or:

\[456 + 570 = 1{,}026\]

The sales tax on the selling price is:

\[1{,}026(0.08) = 82.08\]

The customer pays the selling price plus the sales tax:

\[1{,}026 + 82.08 = 1{,}108.08\]

This formula can be used to determine \(d\), the number of days needed to read \(b\) total pages, reading an average of \(p\) pages per day, with \(e\) extra days taken off for breaks.

\[d = \dfrac{1}{p}b + e\]

If the formula is solved for \(b\), what is the formula?

options.C: \(b = e + pd\)

solution.exhibit_text: Subtract \(e\) from both sides: \(d - e = \dfrac{1}{p}b\). Multiply both sides by \(p\): \(p(d-e) = b\), so \(b = p(d-e)\).

base_question.question:
This formula can be used to determine \(p\), the number of pages that will be in a book that contains \(w\) words, with an average of \(r\) words per page, and \(f\) extra pages in the front for the title and publishing information.

\[p = \dfrac{1}{r}w + f\]

If the formula is solved for \(w\), it can be used to find the number of words in a book with \(p\) pages. What will the formula be if it is solved for \(w\)?

options.C: \(w = f + rp\)

solution.exhibit_text:
(A) Apply the properties of equality to solve for \(w\).

\[p = \dfrac{1}{r}w + f\]

Subtract \(f\) from both sides of the equation.

\[p - f = \dfrac{1}{r}w\]

Multiply both sides by \(r\).

\[r(p - f) = r\left(\dfrac{1}{r}w\right)\]
\[r(p - f) = w\]
\[w = r(p - f)\]

base_question.question: In the pyramid above, each triangular face has the same area, and the base \(MNPQ\) is a square that measures \(8\) centimeters on each side. If the length of \(\overline{RS} = 6\) centimeters, what is the surface area of the pyramid **excluding** the base?

solution.exhibit_text:

Use the information to find the area of **triangle** \(QRP\):

\[A = \tfrac{1}{2}bh = \tfrac{1}{2}(8)(6) = 24 \text{ sq cm.}\]

There are \(4\) congruent triangles in the pyramid, so the surface area of the pyramid **excluding** the base is \(4 \times 24 = 96\) sq cm.

base_question.question: Bryana bought \(1\tfrac{3}{4}\) yards of cloth at $\(8.00\) per yard. If there was an \(8\%\) sales tax, what was the total cost of the cloth?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) Calculate the cost of the cloth before tax:

\[1\tfrac{3}{4} \times 8 = \dfrac{7}{4} \times 8 = 14\]

Find the tax for $\(14\) worth of cloth:

\[14 \times 8\% = 14 \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 1.12\]

Add the cost of the cloth and the tax:

\[14 + 1.12 = 15.12\]

math_questions.question: Each of two spinners is divided into \(5\) equal sections, numbered \(1\) through \(5\). Both spinners are spun once. What is the probability that the two numbers, when multiplied together, will have \(6\) as a product?

solution.exhibit_text: There are \(5 \times 5 = 25\) possible outcomes. The pairs with a product of \(6\) (using numbers \(1\)-\(5\)) are \((2,3)\) and \((3,2)\) — only \(2\) outcomes. The probability is \(\dfrac{2}{25}\).

base_question.question: Karl has one red spinner and one blue spinner. Each spinner is divided into \(4\) equal sections, numbered \(1\) through \(4\). He spins each spinner once and writes down the number that each lands on. What is the probability that the two numbers, when multiplied together, will have \(4\) as a product?

solution.exhibit_text:
(B) There are four possible outcomes for each spin of the spinner:

\(1, 2, 3, 4\)

The possible outcomes of two spins are:

\(11 \quad 12 \quad 13 \quad \boxed{14}\)
\(21 \quad \boxed{22} \quad 23 \quad 24\)
\(31 \quad 32 \quad 33 \quad 34\)
\(\boxed{41} \quad 42 \quad 43 \quad 44\)

Of the \(16\) possible outcomes, **only** \(3\) pairings have a product of \(4\): \(14\), \(22\), and \(41\).

Therefore, the probability that the two numbers resulting from two consecutive spins have a product of \(4\) is \(\dfrac{3}{16}\).

math_questions.question: Point \(X\) is **not** on line \(k\). How many lines can be drawn through \(X\) that form a \(90\degree\) angle with line \(k\)?

options.D: Cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.exhibit_text: A line drawn from \(X\) perpendicular to line \(k\) creates two \(90\degree\) angles. Any other line through \(X\) will not be perpendicular to \(k\), so only one line meets the condition.

base_question.question: Point P is **not** on line \(m\). How many lines can be drawn through P that form a \(90\degree\) angle with line \(m\)?

options.D: Cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.exhibit_text:
Draw a picture to better visualize the situation.

As you can see, a line drawn from P perpendicular to line \(m\) will create two \(90\degree\) angles. However, a line drawn anywhere else will no longer be perpendicular and therefore will not create any \(90\degree\) angles, so only one line meets the conditions of the question.

math_questions.question: If \(4b=12a\), what is the value of \(\dfrac{1}{2}b+5(2b+6)-a\) in terms of \(a\)?

solution.exhibit_text: Solve \(4b=12a\) for \(b\): \(b=3a\). Substitute into the expression: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(3a)+5[2(3a)+6]-a\). The first term is \(1.5a\). Expand the second: \(5(6a+6)=30a+30\). Combine: \(1.5a+30a+30-a=30.5a+30\).

base_question.question: If \(2b=10a\), what is the value of \(\dfrac{1}{2}b+6(2b+7)-a\) in terms of \(a\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
You are given an equation and are tasked with rewriting it in terms of \(a\) (in other words, getting rid of \(b\) and simplifying).

Since you are asked to find the answer "in terms of \(a\)," figure out what \(b\) is in terms of \(a\) by solving \(2b=10a\) for \(b\) and then plug that value into \(\dfrac{1}{2}b+6(2b+7)-a\):

\[2b=10a\]
\[b=\dfrac{10a}{2}\]
\[b=5a\]

Now that you have a value for \(b\), substitute it into the expression.

\[\dfrac{1}{2}b+6(2b+7)-a=\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)(5a)+6[2(5a)+7]-a\]

Simplify the expression piece by piece.

The first term becomes \(\dfrac{1}{2}\times5a=\dfrac{5}{2}a=2.5a\)

Expand the parentheses in the second term: \(6(10a+7)=60a+42\)

The third term remains \(-a\)

You can confidently eliminate (A) and (B) since they have the wrong value for the constant \(42\).

Finally, combine like terms: \(2.5a+60a+42-a=(2.5+60-1)a+42=61.5a+42\), which matches choice (D).

math_questions.question: Marcus has a piece of fabric measuring \(54\) inches by \(90\) inches. He wants to cut it into squares of equal size, without any fabric left over. What is the **greatest** possible side length, in inches, of one of those squares?

solution.exhibit_text: The greatest possible side length is the greatest common factor of the length and width. \(54 = 2\times3\times3\times3\) and \(90=2\times3\times3\times5\). The common factors are \(2\times3\times3=18\). The greatest possible side length is \(18\) in.

base_question.question: Anise has a piece of cloth measuring \(45\) inches by \(75\) inches. She wants to cut it into squares of equal size, without any cloth left over. What is the **greatest** possible side length, in inches, of one of those squares?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) Given that each piece will be a square, the length and width will be the same. The greatest possible length can be determined by finding the greatest common factor of the length and width of the original piece of cloth.

Begin by finding the prime factorization of the length (\(75\) in.) and width (\(45\) in.).

\[45 = 3 \times 3 \times 5\]
\[75 = 3 \times 5 \times 5\]

The common factors can be seen as \(3 \times 5\).

The greatest possible side length, in inches, will be \(3 \times 5 = 15\).

math_questions.question: A gardener has a plot of land that is \(20\) feet by \(30\) feet. If both sides of the plot are increased by \(10\%\), how many square feet will be added to the plot?

solution.exhibit_text: Original area: \(20\times30=600\) sq ft. New dimensions: \(20\times1.10=22\) ft and \(30\times1.10=33\) ft. New area: \(22\times33=726\) sq ft. Added area: \(726-600=126\) sq ft.

base_question.question: A gardener has a plot of land that is \(10\) feet by \(20\) feet. If both sides of the plot are increased by \(20\%\), how many square feet will be added to the plot?

solution.exhibit_text:
Start by finding the total area of the plot before it increases. Plug the original dimensions into the area equation, \(\text{Area}=\text{length}\times\text{width}\), to find that \(\text{Area}=10\times20=200\).

Next, find the new lengths for the plot. To make the math easier, find \(10\%\) and double it to get to \(20\%\). Start with the side length that is \(10\) feet. \(10\%\) of \(10\) is \(1\), so \(20\%\) of \(10\) is \(2\). The new length is \(10+2=12\). Do the same for the other side length. \(10\%\) of \(20\) is \(2\), so \(20\%\) of \(20\) is \(4\). The new length is \(20+4=24\).

The new area is \(12\times24=288\). Finally, subtract the starting area from the new area to find how many square feet the plot increased by: \(288-200=88\).

solution.exhibit_text: Convert 5 ft 3 in. to inches: \(5(12)+3=63\) inches. Multiply by the conversion: \(63 \times 2.54 = 160.02\) cm.

base_question.question: Using the approximation \(2.54\) centimeters \(= 1\) inch, how many centimeters are in \(4\) feet \(7\) inches?

solution.exhibit_text:
(D) Convert \(4\) ft \(7\) in. to inches.

Since \(12\) in. \(= 1\) ft

\[4(12) + 7 = 55 \text{ inches}\]

Multiply that by the conversion:

math_questions.question: What is the probability of rolling a number greater than \(4\) twice in a row on a fair six-sided die, with each of the numbers 1–6 on each side?

solution.exhibit_text: Numbers greater than \(4\) are \(5\) and \(6\): \(2\) out of \(6\), so the probability on one roll is \(\dfrac{2}{6}=\dfrac{1}{3}\). For two rolls in a row, multiply: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{9}\).

base_question.question: What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 3 twice in a row on a fair six-sided die, with each of the numbers 1–6 on each side?

solution.exhibit_text: To find the probability of two independent events, find the probability of each individual event and then multiply those probabilities together. Remember that \(\text{Probability}=\dfrac{\text{Number of Desired Outcomes}}{\text{Number of Total Outcomes}}\). You need to find the probability of rolling a 4, 5, or 6 on the die and then multiply that number by itself. In this scenario, there are 3 desired outcomes out of a total of 6, so the probability of rolling a 4, 5, or 6 is \(\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{1}{2}\). Multiply this number by itself to obtain \(\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{4}\).

math_questions.question: At summer camp, campers are randomly assigned to one of \(20\) cabins and one of \(5\) cafeterias. Omar likes \(5\) of the cabins and \(3\) of the cafeterias. What is the probability that he is assigned to both a cabin and a cafeteria that he likes?

solution.exhibit_text: The probability of a liked cabin is \(\dfrac{5}{20}\), and the probability of a liked cafeteria is \(\dfrac{3}{5}\). Multiply: \(\dfrac{5}{20}\times\dfrac{3}{5}=\dfrac{15}{100}\), or \(15\%\).

base_question.question: At summer camp, campers are randomly assigned to one of 25 cabins and one of 4 cafeterias. Josef likes 8 of the cabins and 2 of the cafeterias. What is the probability that he is assigned to both a cabin and a cafeteria that he likes?

solution.exhibit_text: To find the probability that Josef likes *both* the cabin and the cafeteria he is assigned, find the probability of each and multiply the results. The probability that he will be assigned one of the 8 out of 25 cabins that he likes is \(\dfrac{8}{25}\), and the probability that he will be assigned one of the 2 out of 4 cafeterias that he likes is \(\dfrac{2}{4}\). The product is \(\dfrac{8}{25} \times \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{16}{100}\), or 16%.

math_questions.question: In the figure above, \(PQRS\) is a parallelogram. The measure of \(\angle PQT\) is \(45\degree\), and the measure of \(\angle PTQ\) is \(80\degree\). What is the measure of \(\angle QRS\)?

options.C: \(75\degree\)

solution.exhibit_text: Find angle QPT in triangle PQT: \(180\degree - 80\degree - 45\degree = 55\degree\). In parallelogram PQRS, angle QPT is congruent to angle QRS, so angle QRS is also \(55\degree\).

math_questions.question: In Priya and Diego's class, extra credit quiz scores range from 0 to 50. Priya took \(5\) quizzes, and her mean score was \(36\). Diego took \(9\) quizzes. If both students have the same total score for their quizzes, what was Diego's mean score?

solution.exhibit_text: Priya's total score: \(36\times5=180\). Diego's total score is the same, \(180\), spread over \(9\) quizzes: \(\dfrac{180}{9}=20\).

base_question.question: In James and Sarah's class, extra credit quiz scores range from 0 to 50. Sarah took 6 quizzes, and her mean score was 40. James took 8 quizzes. If both students have the same total score for their quizzes, what was James's mean score?

solution.exhibit_text: Recall that \(\text{Average}=\dfrac{\text{Sum of Values}}{\text{Number of Values}}\). Sarah took 6 quizzes, and her mean was 40, so \(40=\dfrac{\text{Sum of Values}}{6}\). Multiply both sides by 6 to obtain \(240=\text{Sum of Values}\), or total score for the quizzes. James took 8 quizzes, and the sum of his quizzes was the same as Sarah's sum. Therefore, James' average is \(\dfrac{240}{8}=30\).

ela_passages.title: The Past and the Future of the Earth's Oldest Trees
ela_passages.author: Alex Ross
ela_passages.citation: From “The Past and the Future of the Earth's Oldest Trees” by Alex Ross from THE NEW YORKER, January 20, 2020. Copyright © 2020 by Condé Nast. All rights reserved.

paragraphs.text: About forty-five hundred years ago, not long after the completion of the Great Pyramid at Giza, a seed of Pinus longaeva, the Great Basin bristlecone pine, landed on a steep slope in what are now known as the White Mountains, in eastern California. The seed may have travelled there on a gust of wind, its flight aided by a winglike attachment to the nut. Or it could have been planted by a bird known as the Clark's nutcracker, which likes to hide pine seeds in caches; nutcrackers have phenomenal spatial memory and can recall thousands of such caches. This seed, however, lay undisturbed. On a moist day in fall, or in the wake of melting snows in spring, a seedling appeared above ground—a stubby one-inch stem with a tuft of bright-green shoots.

Most seedlings die within a year; the mortality rate is more than ninety-nine percent. The survivors are sometimes seen growing in the shadow of a fallen tree. The landscape of the Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest, as this area of the White Mountains is called, is littered with fragments of dead trees—trunks, limbs, roots, and smaller chunks. Pinus longaeva grows exclusively in subalpine regions of the Great Basin, which stretches from the eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada to the Wasatch Range, in Utah. Conditions are generally too arid for the dead wood to rot; instead, it erodes, sanded down like rock. The remnants may harbor nutrients and fungi that help new trees grow. Bristlecones rise from the bones of their ancestors—a city within a cemetery.

Coast redwoods and giant sequoias, California's gargantuan world-record-holding trees, can grow fifty feet or more in their first twenty years. Bristlecones rise agonizingly slowly. After four or five years, the seedling on the steep slope would have been just a few inches higher, sprouting needles in place of the embryonic shoots. The needles are a deep green, tough, resinous, and closely bunched in groups of five. On a mature tree, they live for fifty years or more. Decades may have passed before the tree was human height, and decades more before it resembled a conventional pine. Bristlecone saplings grow straight up, with relatively sparse foliage, looking like undernourished Christmas trees. After a few hundred years—by which time the Old Kingdom of Egypt had fallen—it was probably forty or fifty feet in height.

Many tree species live for hundreds of years. A smaller but not inconsiderable number, including the sequoias and certain yews, oaks, cypresses, and junipers, survive for thousands. Once a bristlecone has established itself in the unforgiving conditions of the White Mountains, it can last almost indefinitely. The trees tend to grow some distance from one another, so fires almost never destroy an entire stand. Because only a few other plant species can handle the dry, cold climate, the bristlecones face little competition. Unlike most plants, they tolerate dolomite soil, which is composed of a chalky type of limestone that is heavily alkaline and low in nutrients. As for insect threats, bristlecone wood is so dense that mountain-pine beetles and other pests can rarely burrow their way into it.

Empires rose and fell; wars raged; . . . and the tree from 2500 B.C. continued its implacable slow-motion existence, adding about two-hundredths of an inch to the diameter of its trunk each year. Minute changes in the tree-ring record make bristlecones an exceptionally useful source of data about changing conditions on Earth. When rains are heavier than normal, the rings widen. When volcanic eruptions cause global cooling, frost rings make the anomaly visible. . . .

As the millennia go by, bristlecones become contorted and wraithlike. The main stem, or leader, dies back. Entire branches, even the trunk itself, become fossils. At first glance, the tree may look dead. Such is the case of the forty-five-hundred-year-old tree that clings to life near the tourist path that now runs through the Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest. Spears of dead wood jut into the air. The trunk is a marbled hulk stripped of bark, like driftwood thrown from a vanished ocean. A ribbon of live bark runs up one side, funneling water and nutrients to clumps of green needles high above. All told, the tree is an unprepossessing specimen; most people march past it without giving it a second glance. . . .

. . . No two super-elderly trees look alike, to the point where they have acquired the characteristics of individuals. Trees are prone to anthropomorphism; we project our dreams and our anxieties onto them. Bristlecones have been called elders, sentinels, sages. The possibility that climate change will cause their extinction has inspired a spate of alarmed news stories, although tree scientists tend to discount the idea that the bristlecones are in immediate danger. They have survived any number of catastrophes in the past; they may survive humanity.

questions.question: What is the effect of comparing groups of bristlecone pines to “a city within a cemetery” (paragraph 2)?

options.A: It illustrates that the new tree's appearance is markedly different from that of mature bristlecone pines.
options.B: It emphasizes the new tree's ability to use resources left by prior generations of bristlecone pines.
options.C: It highlights the tree's capacity for a long life if it is able to survive to maturity.
options.D: It reveals that the tree's dense growth patterns are unusual in arid conditions.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The reference to “a city within a cemetery” describes how new trees use the remnants of their “ancestors” (paragraph 2) and makes no comment on the appearance of young versus mature trees. B. CORRECT. The “cemetery” contains “the bones of their ancestors” (paragraph 2)—“ancestors” being earlier generations of bristlecone pines—which provide some of the nutrients that the new trees need. C. Incorrect. The reference to “a cemetery” is not a comment on how long bristlecone pines can live; rather, it illustrates that the new pines are using remnants of their “ancestors” (paragraph 2) to grow. D. Incorrect. Although the climate is mentioned in paragraph 2, it is not the reason for the comparison to “a city within a cemetery.” The comment is intended to illustrate how the new trees use nutrients left behind by the old ones.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the idea that the bristlecone pine can withstand difficult conditions is illustrated mainly through

options.A: a comparison of the bristlecone pine with similar trees that are known for their long lives.
options.B: a description of specific qualities of the bristlecone pine that make it suited to its environment.
options.C: an explanation of why the White Mountains are the best place for the bristlecone pine to grow.
options.D: an examination of why the bristlecone pine has few competitors in the White Mountains.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. While paragraph 4 does mention the bristlecone pine in conjunction with other long-living trees, this does not explain in any way how the bristlecone pine can survive difficult conditions. B. CORRECT. Paragraph 4 mentions several qualities that help the bristlecone pine survive a difficult environment: it can survive in a “dry, cold climate” as few plants can, it tolerates a soil that is heavily alkaline and low in nutrients, and the density of its wood protects it from insects. C. Incorrect. Paragraph 4 focuses on the qualities of the bristlecone pine that make it well suited to the White Mountains rather than on why the White Mountains are well suited to bristlecone pines. D. Incorrect. While paragraph 4 does acknowledge that the bristlecone pine has few competitors because the pine can stand conditions few other plants can stand, it is the examination of the pine's unique qualities that explains how the pine survives those conditions.

questions.question: Read this sentence from paragraph 5. “Empires rose and fell; wars raged; . . . and the tree from 2500 B.C. continued its implacable slow-motion existence, adding about two-hundredths of an inch to the diameter of its trunk each year.” The sentence contributes to the development of ideas in the excerpt by

options.A: emphasizing the bristlecone pine's precise growth pattern.
options.B: suggesting that things that seem well established face threats.
options.C: describing the pace of the life cycle of the bristlecone pine.
options.D: explaining the reason for the bristlecone pine's longevity.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. While “two-hundredths of an inch” is a reference to the bristlecone pine's growth pattern, the point of the reference—and of the entire sentence—is to emphasize the incredibly slow pace of the pine's life cycle. B. Incorrect. While “wars raged” is a threat that empires face, the point of mentioning wars and the rise and fall of empires is to emphasize the bristlecone pine's slow-paced life cycle by contrasting its slowness with the big, dramatic changes taking place in human history during that life cycle. C. CORRECT. Making reference to huge changes in human history such as the rise and fall of empires and the raging of wars provides a sharp contrast to the incredibly slow growth of the bristlecone pine. D. Incorrect. This sentence describes how slowly the bristlecone pine grows in contrast to how dramatically human history changes in the same time span but never explains the reasons for the pine's longevity.

questions.question: Which claim is best supported by the details in paragraph 5 about the bristlecone pine's tree-ring record?

options.A: The bristlecone pine must be protected from extinction so that there is a record of changing Earth conditions.
options.B: The structure of the bristlecone pine allows scientists to predict changing Earth conditions over time.
options.C: The slow growth process of the bristlecone pine allows it to survive in spite of changing Earth conditions.
options.D: The bristlecone pine can be used to gather information on changing Earth conditions because of its long life.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. In paragraph 5, the author explains that the bristlecone pine is “an exceptionally useful source of data about changing conditions on Earth,” and this suggests that the information presented by the trees is particularly valuable and important. However, while the paragraph explains that the data provided by the trees are important, it does not address the need to protect the trees from any threat of extinction. The only reference to the trees' extinction is in paragraph 7, when the author addresses the “possibility that climate change will cause their extinction” but then explains that “scientists tend to discount the idea that the bristlecones are in immediate danger.” B. Incorrect. Paragraph 5 describes “minute changes in the tree-ring record” that make bristlecone pines “an exceptionally useful source of data about changing conditions on Earth,” and examples of those changing conditions are described in the present tense: “When rains are heavier than normal, the rings widen.” However, the term “record” indicates that the tree rings are already formed by the time scientists study them. The trees provide information about the past, which is emphasized by the description at the beginning of paragraph 5 of historic events one tree lived through. The excerpt contains no information about whether scientists can use the climate patterns of the past as evidenced by tree rings to make predictions about the future. C. Incorrect. Paragraph 5 describes the “slow-motion existence” of the bristlecone pine and provides examples of the record of “changing conditions on Earth” reflected in the rings of the trees. However, although the paragraph makes it clear that the trees have been able to survive these changing conditions, the paragraph does not indicate that the slow growth of the trees, each of which adds only “about two-hundredths of an inch to the diameter of its trunk each year,” is the key to their survival. Instead, paragraph 4 lists other reasons why an established bristlecone pine “can last almost indefinitely,” including distance between individual trees; tolerance for cold, dry conditions and dolomite soil; and bark that is resistant to insects. D. CORRECT. Paragraph 5 emphasizes the longevity of the bristlecone pine by discussing its “implacable slow-motion existence” and how this makes the trees a valuable source of information for scientists. The author explains that “minute changes in the tree-ring record make bristlecone pines an exceptionally useful source of data about changing conditions on Earth.” A tree that has been alive since 2500 B.C., like the one in paragraph 5, can provide a long record of the changing climate.

questions.question: The phrases “clings to life” and “stripped of bark” in paragraph 6 are used to highlight

options.A: that the tree is fragile and needs help to avoid becoming extinct.
options.B: how the tree can be misunderstood because of its appearance.
options.C: how the tree interests observers with its unusual appearance.
options.D: that the tree manages to survive even when partially fossilized.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. While these two phrases are suggestive of the tree's fragility, nothing in this paragraph suggests that the tree needs help to avoid extinction. B. Incorrect. While the tree may be misunderstood to be dead because it is “stripped of bark,” the phrase “clings to life” emphasizes the fact that the tree is not dead but manages to survive. C. Incorrect. The paragraph says that far from being interested in the tree's unusual appearance, “most people march past it without giving it a second glance” (paragraph 6). D. CORRECT. The phrase “clings to life” emphasizes that the tree is still surviving even though it is partially fossilized, as shown by its “marbled hulk stripped of bark” (paragraph 6).

questions.question: What is the best summary of the bristlecone pine's life cycle?

options.A: The bristlecone pine takes root as a stubby seedling in the mountains. Over time, it grows slowly in a hostile environment with alkaline soil that ensures little competition from other trees.
options.B: The bristlecone pine grows up slowly from the fragments of its dead ancestors. Over time, it begins to become contorted in appearance but continues to funnel water and nutrients to its stem.
options.C: The bristlecone pine grows slowly in an environment hostile to other trees. Over time, its trunk and some branches fossilize, but it funnels water and nutrients to other parts that are still alive.
options.D: The bristlecone pine grows only in one location in the mountains. Over time, it develops sparse foliage that fossilizes slowly, but the trunk and branches stay alive, as revealed by ribbons of live bark.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect—covers minor details and leaves out the fossilization stage of the life cycle described in paragraph 6. B. Incorrect—does not address the fossilization phase accurately and incorrectly states the tree continues to funnel nutrients to its stem rather than to living needles. C. CORRECT—describes the key phases of the life cycle (slow growth in a hostile environment, followed by fossilization of the trunk and some branches while other parts remain alive) without focusing on minor details, and in chronological order. D. Incorrect—focuses on location and appearance more than on the phases of the life cycle.

questions.question: Throughout the excerpt, the author conveys his point of view mainly by

options.A: sharing details about the qualities of the bristlecone pine that make it an unusual tree.
options.B: comparing the bristlecone pine to global empires that lasted thousands of years before falling.
options.C: explaining the way the seemingly sickly appearance of the bristlecone pine contrasts with its ability to survive.
options.D: arguing that the bristlecone pine has survived past threats to its survival and will continue to thrive.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. The author shares many details throughout the excerpt showing how unusual the tree is: it uses remnants from previous generations (paragraph 2), it grows “agonizingly” slowly (paragraph 3), and it survives difficult growing conditions (paragraph 4). B. Incorrect. The author briefly compares the tree to empires (paragraphs 1, 3, 5), but mainly offers many details about what makes the tree unusual. C. Incorrect. Paragraph 6 focuses on the sickly appearance versus survival contrast, but that is just one detail among many. D. Incorrect. Paragraph 7's statement that the trees “may survive humanity” is just one detail among many, not the main way the author conveys his point of view.

paragraphs.text: In the 1950s people compared running one mile in four minutes to scaling Mount Everest and nicknamed the feat a “dream mile.” Although such an accomplishment was considered humanly impossible, several elite runners aimed to break that supposedly impenetrable barrier. One of them was a twenty-five-year-old medical student named Roger Bannister.

Roger Bannister had tasted failure during the 1952 Olympics. There, he was favored to win the 1,500-meter competition, a distance slightly shorter than a mile, but he finished in a dismal fourth place instead. Bannister's performance was a disappointment for him and his country, Great Britain. Determined to redeem himself, Bannister postponed his plans to retire from racing and focused on the ultimate prize—breaking the four-minute-mile barrier.

Bannister attacked the elusive milestone with a positive attitude and logical planning. The amateur athlete decided to use intensive interval training to develop endurance and speed. For these workouts, Bannister ran an interval of ten consecutive laps on a quarter-mile track, aiming for sixty seconds each lap. In between intervals, he let his body recover for two minutes.

By early 1954, Bannister had succeeded in lowering his quarter-mile pace to sixty-one seconds, but he had to shave off at least one more second in order to reach his target. Frustrated by the plateau he had reached, Bannister took a break from training and went mountain climbing for three days. The rest from running permitted his muscles to recuperate and left him feeling refreshed. When Bannister returned to the track, he completed ten quarter-mile-long intervals at fifty-nine seconds each. He finally felt prepared to attempt to break the world record.

As a member of the Amateur Athletic Association (AAA), Bannister joined the AAA team for a track meet against Oxford University. The event took place on a cinder track in Oxford on May 6, 1954. Bannister and his two AAA teammates, Chris Chataway and Chris Brasher, were close friends and frequent running partners. Chataway and Brasher agreed to help Bannister accomplish his goal by being his “rabbits.”

In track and field, rabbits are runners who enter the race solely to pace a teammate for a segment of the course. Typically, a runner settles in behind the rabbit and allows the rabbit to set an appropriate tempo. Additionally, by running behind the rabbit, the runner conserves about 15 percent of his or her effort. When the starting pistol fired, Brasher pounced into the lead, and Bannister followed behind his first rabbit.

Propelled by the excitement, Bannister lost his instinctive feel for his pace and shouted “Faster!” at Brasher. Brasher, however, remained composed and maintained his current steady but grueling pace, completing the first two laps in a desirable one minute and fifty-eight seconds. Then Chataway surged forward, leading Bannister at this same punishing rate for another lap and a half. At the beginning of the back straightaway of the track, Bannister bolted past Chataway. Bannister said, “I felt that the moment of a lifetime had come. There was no pain, only a great unity of movement and aim.” Bannister crossed the finish line in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds. The ecstatic crowd erupted the moment the timekeeper announced the word “three.”

Soon after Bannister's achievement, four other athletes matched his performance. A new mindset had taken root among runners. Over the years, the record continued to fall. However, the current record, 3 minutes 43.13 seconds, has stood unbroken since 1999. Some question whether this record represents the limits of human ability. But perhaps there is another Bannister, an athlete who, with willpower and dedication, will accomplish the miraculous.

questions.question: The words “feat,” “humanly impossible,” and “impenetrable barrier” in paragraph 1 affect the tone of the paragraph because they

options.A: highlight the idea that only the most skilled runners would be able to run a four-minute mile.
options.B: emphasize the idea that running a mile in less than four minutes was a seemingly unattainable goal.
options.C: convey the competitiveness among elite runners to consistently set and break speed records.
options.D: show the intensity of the training programs athletes endure in order to achieve their goals.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. These words suggest the feat was unattainable even for the most skilled runners, which overstates the point. B. CORRECT. No one had ever run a sub-four-minute mile; these words imply the goal seemed unattainable, reinforcing the comparison to “scaling Mount Everest.” C. Incorrect. The paragraph focuses on Bannister specifically, not competitiveness among elite runners in general. D. Incorrect. The training program is described in paragraphs 3-4; these words relate to the magnitude of the goal itself, not the intensity of training.

questions.question: Read these sentences from paragraph 7. “Bannister said, ‘I felt that the moment of a lifetime had come. There was no pain, only a great unity of movement and aim.’” The sentences contribute to the development of ideas in the passage by showing that Bannister

options.A: knew that he was about to achieve the goal he had worked toward.
options.B: was no longer experiencing personal disappointment from his past failure in the Olympics.
options.C: felt grateful to his teammates for helping him take the lead.
options.D: was satisfied that his training had helped him perfect his running technique.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. Bannister's sense that “the moment of a lifetime had come” and the feeling of “unity of movement and aim” reveal his awareness that he was on the verge of achieving his long-sought goal. B,C,D. Incorrect — the lines focus on Bannister's realization that his goal was within reach, not on resolving past disappointment, gratitude toward teammates, or technique.

questions.question: Which sentence best supports the idea that Bannister needed an alternative to “logical planning” (paragraph 3) in order to accomplish his goal?

options.A: “Bannister's performance was a disappointment for him and his country, Great Britain.” (paragraph 2)
options.B: “The amateur athlete decided to use intensive interval training to develop endurance and speed.” (paragraph 3)
options.C: “For these workouts, Bannister ran an interval of ten consecutive laps on a quarter-mile track, aiming for sixty seconds each lap.” (paragraph 3)
options.D: “Frustrated by the plateau he had reached, Bannister took a break from training and went mountain climbing for three days.” (paragraph 4)

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the 1952 Olympics outcome prompted a new goal, not an alternative training method. B. Incorrect — describes his training plan itself, not an alternative to it. C. Incorrect — details of the interval training plan, not an alternative form of preparation. D. CORRECT — explains Bannister reached a point where he couldn't improve despite his strict plan; the mountain-climbing break “permitted his muscles to recuperate and left him feeling refreshed” (paragraph 4) — this is the alternative to logical planning.

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage indicates that Bannister nearly made a mistake that would have cost him the world record?

options.A: “By early 1954, Bannister had succeeded in lowering his quarter-mile pace to sixty-one seconds, but he had to shave off at least one more second in order to reach his target.” (paragraph 4)
options.B: “When the starting pistol fired, Brasher pounced into the lead, and Bannister followed behind his first rabbit.” (paragraph 6)
options.C: “Propelled by the excitement, Bannister lost his instinctive feel for his pace and shouted ‘Faster!’ at Brasher.” (paragraph 7)
options.D: “At the beginning of the back straightaway of the track, Bannister bolted past Chataway.” (paragraph 7)

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — describes a training challenge, not a race mistake. B. Incorrect — describes the start of the race going to plan. C. CORRECT — if Bannister had run faster than the rabbit's pace he'd have lacked the energy to finish; he “lost his instinctive feel for his pace” in excitement, a near mistake. D. Incorrect — describes Bannister moving ahead of the second rabbit at the appropriate, planned time, not a mistake.

questions.question: Bannister's loss in the 1952 Olympics influenced his decision to pursue breaking the four-minute-mile barrier by

options.A: allowing him to recognize his weaknesses and improve his running ability.
options.B: prompting him to take a different approach to his regular training.
options.C: motivating him to prove to himself that he could set and achieve a goal.
options.D: giving him the opportunity to reach a goal no runner had ever accomplished.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the loss made him “determined to redeem himself” and focus specifically on the four-minute mile, not just general improvement. B. Incorrect — the different training approach came later (the 1954 plateau), not directly from the Olympics loss. C. CORRECT — he sought redemption after his “dismal fourth place,” responding by setting a goal to conquer the “ultimate prize” (the four-minute mile). D. Incorrect — the loss motivated a change in focus, not an “opportunity” itself.

ela_passages.title: In Search of the Unknown
ela_passages.author: Robert W. Chambers
ela_passages.citation: From IN SEARCH OF THE UNKNOWN by Robert W. Chambers—Public Domain

paragraphs.text: It was at that time the policy of the trustees and officers of the Zoological Gardens neither to employ collectors nor to send out expeditions in search of specimens. The society decided to depend upon voluntary contributions, and I was always busy, part of the day, in dictating answers to correspondents who wrote offering their services as hunters of big game, collectors of all sorts of fauna, trappers, snarers, and also to those who offered specimens for sale, usually at exorbitant rates.

To the proprietors of . . . mangy lynxes, moth-eaten coyotes, and dancing bears I returned courteous but uncompromising refusals—of course, first submitting all such letters, together with my replies, to Professor Farrago.

One day towards the end of May, however, just as I was leaving Bronx Park to return to town, Professor Lesard, of the reptilian department, called out to me that Professor Farrago wanted to see me a moment; so I . . . retraced my steps to the temporary, wooden building occupied by Professor Farrago, general superintendent of the Zoological Gardens. The professor, who was sitting at his desk before a pile of letters and replies submitted for approval by me, pushed his glasses down and looked over them at me with a whimsical smile that suggested amusement, impatience, annoyance, and perhaps a faint trace of apology.
“Now, here's a letter,” he said, with a deliberate gesture towards a sheet of paper impaled on a file—“a letter that I suppose you remember.” He disengaged the sheet of paper and handed it to me.
“Oh yes,” I replied, with a shrug; “of course the man is mistaken—or—”
“Or what?” demanded Professor Farrago, tranquilly, wiping his glasses.
“—Or a liar,” I replied.

After a silence he leaned back in his chair and bade me read the letter to him again, and I did so with a contemptuous tolerance for the writer, who must have been either a very innocent victim or a very stupid swindler. I said as much to Professor Farrago, but, to my surprise, he appeared to waver.
“I suppose,” he said, with his near-sighted, embarrassed smile, “that nine hundred and ninety-nine men in a thousand would throw that letter aside and condemn the writer as a liar or a fool?”
“In my opinion,” said I, “he's one or the other.”
“He isn't—in mine,” said the professor, placidly.
“What!” I exclaimed. “Here is a man living all alone on a strip of rock and sand between the wilderness and the sea, who wants you to send somebody to take charge of a bird that doesn't exist!”
“How do you know,” asked Professor Farrago, “that the bird in question does not exist?”
“It is generally accepted,” I replied, sarcastically, “that the great auk has been extinct for years. Therefore I may be pardoned for doubting that our correspondent possesses a pair of them alive.”
“Oh, you young fellows,” said the professor, smiling wearily, “you embark on a theory for destinations that don't exist.”
He leaned back in his chair, his amused eyes searching space for the imagery that made him smile.
“Like swimming squirrels, you navigate with the help of Heaven and a stiff breeze, but you never land where you hope to—do you?”
Rather red in the face, I said: “Don't you believe the great auk to be extinct?”
“Audubon saw the great auk.”
“Who has seen a single specimen since?”
“Nobody—except our correspondent here,” he replied, laughing.
I laughed, too, considering the interview at an end, but the professor went on, coolly:
“Whatever it is that our correspondent has—and I am daring to believe that it is the great auk itself—I want you to secure it for the society.”
When my astonishment subsided my first conscious sentiment was one of pity. Clearly, Professor Farrago was on the verge of dotage—ah, what a loss to the world!

I believe now that Professor Farrago perfectly interpreted my thoughts, but he betrayed neither resentment nor impatience. I drew a chair up beside his desk—there was nothing to do but to obey, and this fool's errand was none of my conceiving.
Together we made out a list of articles necessary for me and itemized the expenses I might incur, and I set a date for my return, allowing no margin for a successful termination to the expedition.
“Never mind that,” said the professor. “What I want you to do is to get those birds here safely. Now, how many men will you take?”
“None,” I replied, bluntly; “it's a useless expense, unless there is something to bring back. If there is I'll wire you, you may be sure.”
“Very well,” said Professor Farrago, good-humoredly, “you shall have all the assistance you may require. Can you leave to-night?”
The old gentleman was certainly prompt. I nodded, half-sulkily, aware of his amusement.
“So,” I said, picking up my hat, “I am to start north to find a place called Black Harbor, where there is a man named Halyard who possesses, among other household utensils, two extinct great auks—”
We were both laughing by this time. I asked him why on earth he credited the assertion of a man he had never before heard of.

“I suppose,” he replied, with the same half-apologetic, half-humorous smile, “it is instinct. I feel, somehow, that this man Halyard has got an auk—perhaps two. I can't get away from the idea that we are on the eve of acquiring the rarest of living creatures. It's odd for a scientist to talk as I do; doubtless you're shocked—admit it, now!”
