But I was not shocked; on the contrary, I was conscious that the same strange hope that Professor Farrago cherished was beginning, in spite of me, to stir my pulses, too.
“If he has—” I began, then stopped.
The professor and I looked hard at each other in silence.
“Go on,” he said, encouragingly.

But I had nothing more to say, for the prospect of beholding with my own eyes a living specimen of the great auk produced a series of conflicting emotions within me which rendered speech profanely superfluous.

questions.question: Read paragraph 2 from the excerpt. “To the proprietors of . . . mangy lynxes, moth-eaten coyotes, and dancing bears I returned courteous but uncompromising refusals—of course, first submitting all such letters, together with my replies, to Professor Farrago.” This paragraph helps develop the plot by establishing that the narrator

options.A: dislikes writing refusal letters for the animals offered to the zoological society.
options.B: attempts to predict what the professor would say in the refusal letters.
options.C: believes that many of the animals offered are not acceptable for the zoological society.
options.D: resents the professor's insistence on reviewing the refusal letters.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The narrator shows no indication of disliking the work; the letters inform people whether the zoo will accept the animals. B. Incorrect. The narrator is confident in his own reply and doesn't anticipate differing from the professor, so there's no need to “predict.” C. CORRECT. “Uncompromising refusals” indicates the narrator's initial confidence that the animals in the letters aren't of value to the society; this confidence is later shaken as the plot unfolds when Professor Farrago states “I am daring to believe that it is the great auk itself” (paragraph 23); the narrator's transition from dismissive doubt to budding hopefulness is a major part of the plot (“But I was not shocked; on the contrary, I was conscious that the same strange hope that Professor Farrago cherished was beginning, in spite of me, to stir my pulses, too” [paragraph 34]). D. Incorrect. The narrator doesn't resent the review; “of course” in paragraph 2 shows he expects to submit letters to the professor as part of his job.

questions.question: Read this sentence from paragraph 3. “The professor, who was sitting at his desk before a pile of letters and replies submitted for approval by me, pushed his glasses down and looked over them at me with a whimsical smile that suggested amusement, impatience, annoyance, and perhaps a faint trace of apology.” What does the phrase “a faint trace of apology” convey about the professor?

options.A: It indicates that the professor feels bad that he has to call the narrator to his office after work.
options.B: It shows that the professor is hesitant to share his opinions with the narrator.
options.C: It implies that the professor is uncomfortable criticizing the narrator's work.
options.D: It suggests that the professor knows that the conversation will be frustrating for the narrator.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The apologetic manner is not about calling the narrator after work; it is caused by the professor's understanding that the conversation about the letter/expedition will cause an argument; in paragraph 29 the professor asks if the narrator can leave on the expedition that evening, showing he doesn't feel bad about taking the narrator's time. B. Incorrect. The paragraphs that follow show the professor sharing opinions without pause even when unflattering (“Like swimming squirrels, you navigate with the help of Heaven and a stiff breeze, but you never land where you hope to—do you?” [paragraph 17]). C. Incorrect. The professor is not uncomfortable challenging the narrator; he seems at ease. D. CORRECT. The professor is amused and annoyed by the narrator's dismissal of the possibility that great auks exist, and he knows the narrator will react negatively to being sent on what the narrator considers a “fool's errand” (paragraph 25).

questions.question: How does the exchange between the professor and the narrator in paragraphs 8-11 contribute to the development of the characters?

options.A: It establishes the conflict between the professor and the narrator concerning the validity of the letter.
options.B: It suggests a theme of collaboration because the narrator and the professor regularly work together.
options.C: It reveals the characters' traits by contrasting the narrator's distrust with how easily the professor is deceived by what he reads.
options.D: It hints that the resolution will involve the narrator accepting the professor's opinion about the content of the letter.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. It reveals the difference in opinions: the narrator believes without doubt that Halyard (the letter writer about the auks) is “a liar or a fool” (paragraph 9), while the professor believes the letter writer could be telling the truth (“I said as much to Professor Farrago, but, to my surprise, he appeared to waver” [paragraph 8]). B. Incorrect. In paragraph 8, the narrator reacts with “contemptuous tolerance” and is shocked the professor agrees with Halyard (paragraph 11), whom the narrator condemned as a liar or fool (paragraph 10)—this is emphatic disagreement, not collaboration. C. Incorrect. The professor is portrayed as experienced and intelligent, not easily deceived. D. Incorrect. Paragraphs 8-11 primarily establish a difference of opinion, not a hint at the resolution.

questions.question: The professor's observations in paragraphs 15-17 create tension in the excerpt by causing the narrator to feel

options.A: flustered by the professor's criticism of his logic.
options.B: annoyed by the professor's sarcasm about his inexperience.
options.C: confused by the professor's lack of respect for his opinion.
options.D: frustrated by the professor's lack of interest in his theory.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. The professor criticizes “you young fellows” (paragraph 15), suggesting the ideas of young scientists like the narrator are unsupported (“like swimming squirrels” [paragraph 17]) and inaccurate (“but you never land where you hope to—do you?” [paragraph 17] and “you embark on a theory for destinations that don't exist” [paragraph 15]). The narrator becomes “rather red in the face” (paragraph 18), indicating he's upset, and asks the professor about the great auk in an attempt to defend himself. B. Incorrect. The narrator has a negative reaction, but the professor is genuine, not sarcastic; sarcasm comes from the narrator in paragraph 14 (“It is generally accepted,” I replied, sarcastically . . .). C. Incorrect. The professor's observations cause the narrator to blush with embarrassment, but the narrator understands the professor's point about the narrator's unquestioning acceptance that great auks don't exist; the professor is criticizing youthful ideas, not disrespecting the narrator's opinion. D. Incorrect. The professor shows amusement with the narrator's perspective; the narrator is embarrassed and upset, but doesn't show frustration with the professor's “lack of interest”—the professor is interested.

questions.question: How does the interaction between the narrator and the professor in paragraphs 26-28 contribute to the development of the theme?

options.A: It illustrates the professor's patience as the narrator argues against making the expedition.
options.B: It reveals the narrator's frustration with his limited role in making decisions for the zoological society.
options.C: It emphasizes the professor's desire to acquire new specimens for the zoological society at any cost.
options.D: It shows the narrator's acceptance of his assignment despite his personal objections.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The narrator doesn't argue against making the expedition; he argues that it's unnecessary for the professor to pay for extra men, since the narrator can ask for assistance if he does find great auks (“None,” I replied, bluntly; “it's a useless expense, unless there is something to bring back. If there is I'll wire you, you may be sure” [paragraph 28]). B. Incorrect. The narrator's frustration/embarrassment comes from the professor criticizing his blind acceptance of a theory, not from an inability to make decisions. C. Incorrect. The professor states “what I want you to do is to get those birds here safely” (paragraph 27), indicating the priority is the birds' safety, not acquiring them at any cost. D. CORRECT. Paragraph 26 describes the professor and narrator making practical plans (“we made out a list of articles necessary for me and itemized the expenses I might incur”), indicating the narrator's acceptance of the assignment while not anticipating a “successful termination.” Paragraph 28 describes the narrator's personal objections (he believes extra men are pointless, “a useless expense”) since he doesn't expect to find any great auks.

questions.question: Which sentence from the excerpt best explains why the professor is eager to send the narrator on an expedition?

options.A: “I believe now that Professor Farrago perfectly interpreted my thoughts, but he betrayed neither resentment nor impatience.” (paragraph 25)
options.B: “Together we made out a list of articles necessary for me and itemized the expenses I might incur, and I set a date for my return, allowing no margin for a successful termination to the expedition.” (paragraph 26)
options.C: “‘What I want you to do is to get those birds here safely.’” (paragraph 27)
options.D: “‘I can't get away from the idea that we are on the eve of acquiring the rarest of living creatures.’” (paragraph 33)

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The narrator suspects the professor is losing his ability to reason since the request seems impossible; this doesn't explain WHY the professor is excited. B. Incorrect. This shows planning logistics, not why the professor is eager. C. Incorrect. This shows interest in the birds' safety but not the underlying reason (rarity). D. CORRECT. This reveals the professor's excitement to get “the rarest of living creatures,” the great auk. In paragraph 14 the narrator states “it is generally accepted . . . that the great auk has been extinct for years,” making a living auk incredibly rare and explaining the professor's eagerness.

questions.question: How does paragraph 34 help develop the plot of the excerpt?

options.A: It shows that the narrator is beginning to consider the possibility of finding the great auks.
options.B: It demonstrates that the narrator is struggling to understand why the professor thinks the great auks exist.
options.C: It establishes that the narrator is willing to let the professor overrule him about the great auks.
options.D: It emphasizes that the narrator feels a sense of urgency to complete the expedition to locate the great auks.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. Despite initial disbelief, the narrator admits in paragraph 34 that he's starting to feel the “same strange hope” the professor feels (paragraph 33). B. Incorrect. Paragraph 34 reveals the narrator is affected by the professor's “strange hope,” beginning to share it “in spite of” himself—not struggling to understand. C. Incorrect. The hope described wouldn't be present if the narrator were simply overruled without sharing the belief; it was already established before paragraph 34 that the narrator was willing to be overruled (“I drew a chair up beside his desk—there was nothing to do but to obey, and this fool's errand was none of my conceiving” [paragraph 25]). D. Incorrect. The narrator doesn't express urgency in paragraph 34; he expresses hope that the auks might really exist.

questions.question: Which sentence best demonstrates the professional relationship between the narrator and the professor?

options.A: “He disengaged the sheet of paper and handed it to me.” (paragraph 4)
options.B: “Clearly, Professor Farrago was on the verge of dotage—ah, what a loss to the world!” (paragraph 24)
options.C: “I drew a chair up beside his desk—there was nothing to do but to obey, and this fool's errand was none of my conceiving.” (paragraph 25)
options.D: “‘Very well,’ said Professor Farrago, good-humoredly, ‘you shall have all the assistance you may require.’” (paragraph 29)

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. This doesn't convey a subordinate/superior relationship. B. Incorrect. This is a momentary reaction, not a demonstration of the professional relationship. C. CORRECT. The narrator disagrees (“this fool's errand was none of my conceiving”) but obeys because he works for the professor (“there was nothing to do but to obey”). D. Incorrect. The professor's good-humored offer doesn't best demonstrate the underlying employer-employee relationship.

questions.question: How does the author develop the contrast between the narrator's point of view and the professor's point of view?

options.A: by providing both the narrator's and professor's thoughts on how age and experience influence each other's reasoning
options.B: by using the conversation between the narrator and the professor to emphasize their reactions to the letter
options.C: by describing the professor's persistent efforts to change the narrator's mind about the letter
options.D: by including dialogue that explains why the professor is the supervisor and the narrator is his subordinate

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The excerpt doesn't describe the narrator's thoughts on age/experience in enough detail. B. CORRECT. The primary conflict revolves around the narrator's disagreement with the professor about whether the letter about the great auks could be true; the narrator dismisses the possibility out of hand (“of course the man is mistaken” [paragraph 5]; “here is a man . . . who wants you to send somebody to take charge of a bird that doesn't exist!” [paragraph 12]), while the professor calmly admits “nine hundred and ninety-nine men in a thousand would throw that letter aside and condemn the writer” (paragraph 9) yet himself believes the writer could be telling the truth (“How do you know,” asked Professor Farrago, “that the bird in question does not exist?” [paragraph 13]). C. Incorrect. The professor explains the disagreement (paragraphs 19-21) but doesn't make persistent efforts to convince the narrator; instead, he states the narrator will go on the expedition regardless of the narrator's belief. D. Incorrect. The dialogue's point isn't to explain the subordinate-supervisor relationship, but to contrast what each character believes about the letter's contents.

ela_passages.title: Looking for the Smallest Spark of Everything

lines.text: There are the things the world is made of,
things we can see and feel, and then
there are the things even smaller, things that seem
to exist only when we are looking right at them.
So beneath the level of molecules are atoms,
and beneath the level of atoms, we find
protons, electrons, neutrons; and beneath that—
what, exactly? Because we are talking about
everything here: your fingernail,
the candy at the back of your mouth,
the coffee your teacher drank this morning,
your little sister, and the stuffed dog
she used to carry around with her everywhere.
And everywhere.
Everything and everywhere
are made up of the same stuff, whatever
it is. How do we find it? We can listen for it
in the wavelengths from deep space,
talking back to us from unimaginable
distances. Or we can build long,
deep circular tunnels beneath the surface
of this Earth and race particles
(like racing cars, only very tiny cars
flashing along at close to the speed of light)
until everything we think we know
bangs against everything else we know.
And there, in the explosion, in the darkness,
briefly incandescent, they appear:
the quarks, the leptons, and the bosons;
the baryons and the mesons. Their names
sound like dinosaurs or maybe bands
playing terrible music in someone's garage.
The one thing we know for sure
is that they spin. This is how gravity
enters our world, how our world is held
both together and apart, what keeps
together the pencil in your hand right now
as well as separate from, say,
Jupiter. They spin, and it is only down there
in the darkness—in the vast garage
where physicists jot down
what they can, whatever seems most real—
that they let us perceive their wild dancing,
combusting to the music they make.

questions.question: Read lines 5-8 from the poem. The lines help develop a central idea of the poem by revealing the speaker's

options.A: interest in determining how the parts of matter work together.
options.B: curiosity about what makes up matter.
options.C: desire to prove that particles make up matter.
options.D: questions about what tools are needed to study matter.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — lines 5-8 demonstrate knowledge about the structure of matter, not interest in how parts work together. B. CORRECT — lines 5-8 show connection between particles using “beneath the level” repeatedly; the progression from atoms to subatomic particles ends with the question “what, exactly?” (line 8), showing the speaker's curiosity about mysteries still unsolved about the nature of matter — a central idea. C. Incorrect — speaker expresses curiosity, not a desire to prove a point; no conflict is shown. D. Incorrect — the poem is about the LHC (a tool) per the intro text, but lines 5-8 specifically are about the particles themselves, not tools.

questions.question: The main purpose of the comparison in lines 23-24 of the poem is to show

options.A: that the particles' size makes them difficult to see.
options.B: how the particles move within the tunnel.
options.C: that the particles have a familiar shape.
options.D: how the particles can be seen only in darkness.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the comparison focuses on movement, not visibility. B. CORRECT — lines 23-24 describe “tiny cars / flashing along at close to the speed of light,” describing how the particles move. C. Incorrect — the lines describe movement, not shape. D. Incorrect — “flashing” refers to speed, not brightness in darkness; “light” is a reference to the measurement of speed.

questions.question: Read lines 27-28 from the poem. The imagery in the lines reveals that the speaker

options.A: envies the physicists who research colliding particles.
options.C: admires the powerful reactions that occur when particles collide.
options.D: has a simplistic understanding of how particles collide.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the physicists in stanza 5 are mere observers; the speaker in lines 27-28 is focused on the reaction, not the physicists. B. Incorrect — the speaker's understanding is based on physicists' observations, not personal witness. C. CORRECT — “explosion” and “briefly incandescent” create a picture of rapid change and bright light, revealing how powerful the new particles are; the positive language shows admiration/awe. D. Incorrect — the poem reveals the speaker's deep knowledge (naming particles, using precise imagery for a complex process), not a simplistic understanding.

questions.question: Read lines 30-32 from the poem. The speaker refers to familiar objects and events in the lines most likely to

options.A: explain confusing information in simple terms to help the reader understand more about the topic.
options.B: demonstrate how scientific ideas can be explained by describing situations that many people are familiar with.
options.C: emphasize that the process being used to research particles is still in the early stages of development.
options.D: suggest that the scientific language used to describe particles seems silly by making a humorous comparison.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the speaker only gives an opinion about the names, not a simplification of confusing information about how particles function. B. Incorrect — only describes what the names sound like, doesn't explain scientific ideas. C. Incorrect — doesn't explain the research process. D. CORRECT — “their names” (line 30) refers to scientific names (quarks, leptons, bosons, baryons, mesons); the speaker opines these sound nonsensical, like dinosaur names or silly band names — a humorous comparison.

questions.question: Read lines 36-39 from the poem. The poet includes these lines most likely to emphasize that

options.A: it is important for physicists to continue their research about particles.
options.B: these particles have a powerful effect on everything.
options.C: the discoveries about particles provide little information.
options.D: the study of particles and the study of objects in space are similar.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the lines explain the power of particles, not the need for more research. B. CORRECT — particles that are “everything and everywhere” (line 15) make up objects in lines 36-39 (a pencil, Jupiter); though different and far apart, both are made of and affected by these particles; the “powerful effect” keeps objects “both together and apart” (line 36). C. Incorrect — discoveries are ongoing and informative, not providing little information. D. Incorrect — the speaker is not comparing the study of particles with the study of space objects; Jupiter is just used as an example object.

questions.question: The imagery in the final stanza of the poem mainly conveys the speaker's

options.A: frustration with the limitations of particle research.
options.B: concern about the dangerous nature of particle collisions.
options.C: interest in physicists and their study of particles.
options.D: doubt about the accuracy of information gathered about particles.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the imagery conveys a positive tone (“perceive their wild dancing,” “combusting to the music they make”), not frustration. B. Incorrect — imagery of energetic movement describes the particles, not danger. C. CORRECT — phrases like “only down there” (line 40), “physicists jot down . . . whatever seems most real” (lines 41-42), and “they let us perceive” (line 43) convey that physicists have a rare role studying the mysteries of the universe; the speaker appreciates and is interested in their work. D. Incorrect — darkness refers to the mysteries of subatomic particles, not secretive physicist work processes.

ela_passages.title: Using Fire to Keep a Prairie Healthy

paragraphs.text: Inside the 40,000-acre Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve in northern Oklahoma, herds of bison roam on the scenic land that is home to hundreds of different species of plants and animals. While one of the greatest threats to the prairie is wildfire, the use of controlled fires is actually an effective way to protect this idyllic landscape.

Fires that are started by lightning or other natural circumstances are inevitable, and the results can be disastrous. However, hundreds of years ago the American Indian people who inhabited the Great Plains area between Minnesota and Texas realized that these fires could also be helpful. The bison in the area seemed to prefer grazing on tender new grass on the recently burned land rather than on grass in the unburned areas. The American Indian people began to deliberately burn areas of land for bison to graze on, which enticed the herds away from the people's crops.

Today conservationists at the Tallgrass Prairie Preserve and farmers in the Great Plains continue to use controlled burns for land management. Intentionally burning a portion of land can dramatically improve the quality of the vegetation that regrows there. The fires burn away weedy undergrowth and help limit the overcrowding of shrubs and trees in the burn area, creating less competition for water and nutrients. Additionally, the process of burning excess plant matter adds nitrogen, an essential element for plant growth, to the soil.

One common target of controlled burns at the preserve and the surrounding area is the invasive red cedar tree. A single red cedar tree can consume up to 40 gallons of water per day, taking this vital resource away from other plant life. These tall trees also cast shade that prevents sunlight from reaching the plants beneath them. The fast-growing red cedar trees tend to crowd out prairie grasses, the primary food source for wild and domestic animals that make the prairie their home. An imbalance in one component of the prairie's ecosystem affects the entire web of life. Controlled burns help maintain this ecosystem's delicate balance.

Of course, these controlled fires are intended to burn only a portion of an area. A total burn, which is a risk with an uncontrolled wildfire, would destroy all wildlife as well as the crops farmers plant for income. The key to using controlled fires is knowing which areas of land to burn and when. Conservation experts at the preserve employ the “patch-burn” approach, meaning they rotate which portion of land is burned each year. They study the land to find out which areas would most benefit from being burned, and then they arrange about a dozen burns over one-third of the land. This patch burning contains the fire within a specific area and allows animals in the burn area to safely relocate. The following year, conservationists will burn a different section of the preserve, while the land burned the previous year regrows healthier than before.

Researchers have tracked and studied the variety of plant species and animals that live on the preserve, and their studies show that the patch-burn approach has restored biodiversity to the area by promoting the growth of species that were at risk of being crowded out. The patch-burn system is so successful that the conservationists at the preserve provide training to prairie farmers about conducting controlled burns on their own land. Burning land to make it healthy may seem counterintuitive, but strategic controlled fires have helped the prairie sustain life for hundreds of years and, with careful management, will continue to do so.

questions.question: According to the passage, how did fires started by natural causes prompt American Indians to begin practicing controlled burns?

options.A: by drawing animals in to the area to feed on the new growth sprouting from the burned land
options.B: by destroying tall trees and reducing the shade that had hindered the growth of planted crops
options.C: by burning off excess vegetation and increasing the availability of nutrients for the remaining plants
options.D: by causing changes to the bison's migration habits as bison herds fled from the wildfires on the prairie

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. Paragraph 2 states American Indians observed bison “grazing on tender new grass on the recently burned land rather than on grass in the unburned areas”—these observations prompted controlled burns to entice “herds away from the people's crops.” B. Incorrect. The paragraph 4 detail about red cedar trees/shade supports why conservationists use controlled burns TODAY, not what initially prompted the practice. C. Incorrect. Paragraph 3 details about nitrogen/soil quality don't explain the initial observations that prompted the practice. D. Incorrect. There's no indication bison changed migration habits to flee wildfires.

questions.question: Targeting red cedar trees in controlled burns affects the animals that live on the prairie mostly by

options.A: ensuring that the animals' main food source has the conditions needed for it to thrive.
options.B: endangering the animals that live near the trees scheduled for removal.
options.C: making sure that the water supply for the animals is sufficient.
options.D: reducing the animals' natural source of shade and protection from the elements.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. Paragraph 4: targeting invasive red cedar trees ensures they don't “crowd out prairie grasses, the primary food source for wild and domestic animals that make the prairie their home”—removing them increases water and sunlight for prairie grasses. B. Incorrect. Paragraph 5: patch burning “allows animals in the burn area to safely relocate”—not endangering. C. Incorrect. The water statistic is about water for the grasses, not directly ensuring sufficient water supply for animals. D. Incorrect. Red cedars are invasive, not a natural part of the ecosystem; shade reduction isn't about animals' comfort/protection.

questions.question: Read this sentence from paragraph 6. “The patch-burn system is so successful that the conservationists at the preserve provide training to prairie farmers about conducting controlled burns on their own land.” The author includes this sentence to show that

options.A: the conservationists are better qualified to lead preservation efforts than farmers are.
options.B: the conservationists are eager to involve others in the preservation of the prairie.
options.C: the conservationists' efforts will restore the original beauty and biodiversity of the region.
options.D: the conservationists' training program should serve as a model for other conservation organizations.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The sentence shows conservationists believe farmers capable of performing controlled burns, not that conservationists are better qualified. B. CORRECT. The conservationists are eager to involve others because “studies show that the patch-burn approach has restored biodiversity to the area by promoting the growth of species that were at risk of being crowded out” and “helped the prairie sustain life for hundreds of years” (paragraph 6); sharing knowledge with people who live on the prairie supports this eagerness. C. Incorrect. The idea that burns restore biodiversity isn't the focus of this specific sentence. D. Incorrect. There's no indication the training program should be a model for OTHER organizations.

questions.question: Which sentence supports the idea that farmers and people who manage land may be concerned about using fire as a way to benefit the land?

options.A: “While one of the greatest threats to the prairie is wildfire, the use of controlled fires is actually an effective way to protect this idyllic landscape.” (paragraph 1)
options.B: “The American Indian people began to deliberately burn areas of land for bison to graze on, which enticed the herds away from the people's crops.” (paragraph 2)
options.C: “This patch burning contains the fire within a specific area and allows animals in the burn area to safely relocate.” (paragraph 5)
options.D: “The following year, conservationists will burn a different section of the preserve, while the land burned the previous year regrows healthier than before.” (paragraph 5)

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. Acknowledges “one of the greatest threats to the prairie is wildfire,” showing why farmers/land managers might be concerned about fire. B, C, D. Incorrect—each explains benefits/mechanics of controlled burns without addressing the underlying concern about fire as a threat.

questions.question: Read this sentence from paragraph 6. “Burning land to make it healthy may seem counterintuitive, but strategic controlled fires have helped the prairie sustain life for hundreds of years and, with careful management, will continue to do so.” The words “counterintuitive” and “strategic” convey the idea that

options.A: the safest methods are sometimes the least effective at solving complex challenges.
options.B: thorough investigation of uncommon methodologies can lead to beneficial results.
options.C: detailed planning can ensure that a potentially destructive action has a positive impact.
options.D: plans that entail a certain amount of risk almost always result in success.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The methods have NOT been ineffective—the patch-burn system is “so successful” conservationists train farmers. B. Incorrect. Doesn't suggest the methodologies are uncommon (they were used by American Indian people long ago). C. CORRECT. Paragraph 1 states “one of the greatest threats to the prairie is wildfire,” so controlled burns suggest risk/counter to common expectations about the dangers of fire; the words convey the idea that detailed planning (“strategic”) can ensure a potentially destructive action (burning) has a positive impact. D. Incorrect. The passage doesn't suggest risky plans “almost always” succeed—success here comes specifically from careful planning.

questions.question: With which statement would the author most likely agree?

options.A: It is important to explain the purposes and the risks of controlled burns to the people living near a proposed burn area.
options.B: It is necessary to thoroughly examine a particular region in order to plan and execute a successful controlled burn.
options.C: Monitoring animals' reactions after a controlled burn on the prairie is a minor part of scientists' research.
options.D: Conservationists should consider the helpful aspects of invasive species before executing a controlled burn.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. In paragraph 5, the author states that “patch burning contains the fire within a specific area and allows animals in the burn area to safely relocate,” and paragraph 6 states that conservationists “provide training to prairie farmers about conducting controlled burns on their own land.” However, the author does not explicitly take a position about the importance of explaining the purposes and risks of controlled burns to people living near a proposed burn area. B. CORRECT. In paragraph 5, the author points out that conservationists “study the land to find out which areas would most benefit from being burned, and then they arrange about a dozen burns over one-third of the land” and “rotate which portion of land is burned each year” so that animals, such as bison, can “safely relocate.” Therefore, the author would most likely agree that it is necessary to thoroughly examine a particular region in order to plan and execute a successful controlled burn. C. Incorrect. The author would be unlikely to agree that monitoring animals' reactions after a controlled burn on the prairie is a minor part of scientists' research. In paragraph 5, the author explains that patch burning “allows animals in the burn area to safely relocate” and that conservationists “burn a different section of the preserve” each year to ensure that animals have an abundant area to graze while other areas are being burned. D. Incorrect. According to the information in paragraph 4, conservationists commonly target invasive red cedar trees because they are tall trees that “crowd out prairie grasses, the primary food source for wild and domestic animals that make the prairie their home.” Since the focus is on the harm that the invasive red cedar trees cause, the author would be unlikely to agree that conservationists should consider helpful aspects of invasive species before a controlled burn.

questions.question: How do the diagram and its text provide additional support for the topic presented in the passage?

options.A: by depicting how the landscape in a given area changes as the patch-burn method is applied
options.B: by indicating that patch-burn fires are best suited for use in areas with certain features
options.C: by revealing that the patch-burn method is used primarily on uninhabited areas of land
options.D: by comparing the size of the area burned by the patch-burn method with that of unburned areas

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. The text of the diagram states that “by using a patch-burn method, conservationists and farmers can reduce the risk of unintentional fires and control where grazing animals, such as bison, roam.” By showing the pattern of controlled burns and the resulting bison migration in a given area, the diagram depicts how the landscape changes as the patch-burn method is applied. B. Incorrect. Although the text mentions areas “where grazing animals, such as bison, roam,” the diagram does not depict distinctive features of the land such as trees or brush and therefore does not indicate that patch-burn fires are best suited for use in areas with certain features. C. Incorrect. While the text mentions “grazing animals, such as bison” and the diagram shows the bison grazing in only one area, the diagram and its text do not indicate that the patch-burn method is used on uninhabited land. D. Incorrect. While the areas of land depicted in the diagram do indicate that the sizes of the areas differ, the text provided does not compare the sizes of the areas burned by the patch-burn method with that of unburned areas.

ela_passages.title: Letter from Brooklyn
ela_passages.author: Jacob Scheier
ela_passages.citation: “Letter from Brooklyn” from LETTER FROM BROOKLYN: POEMS by Jacob Scheier, published by ECW Press. Copyright © 2013 by Jacob Scheier. All rights reserved.

lines.text: I can already see how this will end.
How I will grow tired of the bridge's
steep incline, and the absent-minded tourists
wandering into the bicycle path.
The weather will turn cold.
But that all happens later.
For now it is the early edge of fall,
leaves green still while the air narrows,
is slightly crisp, almost grazing
the hair of my arm like a passing stranger,
as though the air has been forced into intimacy
by the brevity of daylight.
But when it starts darkening at 4,
this closeness, I know, will be a felt distance,
like someone drawing your attention
to their lack of intimacy.
These days I am still walking at a cathedral pace
beneath the branches bending across avenues,
brownstones like rows of lived-in chapels,
like a pop-up picture book I could have had as a child,
but didn't. How Brooklyn makes me nostalgic
for the moment I am walking inside of.
These late afternoons filled
with a loneliness that makes me feel
distinctly myself, and an awareness
of how rare that is.

questions.question: How does the structure of the poem affect the poem's meaning?

options.A: The lack of a rhyming pattern suggests that the beauty of each passing day is unique.
options.B: The lengths of the sentences represent the complexity of the thoughts being represented.
options.C: The use of complete sentences implies the speaker's appreciation for the clear beginning and ending of each season.
options.D: The single long stanza reflects the continuous flow of the speaker's thoughts.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the poem's lack of rhyme is not related to the uniqueness of passing days; the poem is primarily concerned with broad seasonal shifts. B. Incorrect — the poem includes both long sentences (lines 7-12) and short sentences (lines 5-6), but sentence lengths aren't connected to the complexity of ideas expressed. C. Incorrect — a complete sentence presents the beginning and end of a single thought, but the poem isn't primarily concerned with the speaker's thoughts on the clear beginning/ending of each season. D. CORRECT — unlike poems broken into stanzas reflecting unified groups of thoughts, this poem is one long stanza, emphasizing the uninterrupted flow of the speaker's thoughts from time to time and experience to experience without a clear break between any specific thoughts.

questions.question: Which lines support the idea that a change in the weather will lessen the speaker's appreciation for the city?

options.A: “as though the air has been forced into intimacy / by the brevity of daylight.” (lines 11-12)
options.B: “But when it starts darkening at 4, / this closeness, I know, will be a felt distance,” (lines 13-14)
options.C: “like someone drawing your attention / to their lack of intimacy.” (lines 15-16)
options.D: “These days I am still walking . . . / beneath the branches bending across avenues,” (lines 17-18)

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — these lines focus on the positive way the air feels during “the early edge of fall” (line 7); they suggest the speaker appreciates this experience currently, while being aware the feeling might not last. B. CORRECT — these lines describe the shift in the “closeness” of the air as the weather changes and “it starts darkening at 4.” The speaker clearly indicates that the positive emotions surrounding this closeness, with “leaves green still” and the air “slightly crisp” (lines 8-9), will soon be “a felt distance,” suggesting the turn in weather will make the city less appealing. C. Incorrect — although these lines compare the darkening weather to a person revealing a “lack of intimacy,” that specific comparison doesn't focus on a diminishing appreciation for the city. D. Incorrect — these lines describe the “cathedral pace” (line 17) at which the speaker walks, emphasizing a meditative or thoughtful experience; such a description suggests the speaker still appreciates the city, not that the speaker's appreciation will lessen.

questions.question: Read lines 5-6 from the poem. “The weather will turn cold. / But that all happens later.” How do the lines develop a central theme of the poem?

options.A: They highlight a contrast between the different seasons.
options.B: They show the sequence of the changes that are expected to occur.
options.C: They warn about a problem that requires thoughtful preparation.
options.D: They emphasize the importance of valuing the present.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the poem describes impressions of one day in one season (“For now it is the early edge of fall, / leaves green still while the air narrows, / is slightly crisp” [lines 7-9]); despite the reference in line 5 to the eventual arrival of cold weather, lines 5-6 primarily emphasize the speaker's wish to stay focused on the present moment. A contrast between seasons is not a central theme of the poem. B. Incorrect — “The weather will turn cold” (line 5) refers to one change that is expected to occur, but lines 5-6 do not show a sequence of changes; the line that follows returns to the present: “For now . . .” (line 7). C. Incorrect — although the statement that the weather “will turn cold” in line 5 could be construed as a warning, there is no support in lines 5-6 for the idea that some problems require thoughtful preparation; the speaker is reflecting on a fleeting experience, not preparing to solve a problem. D. CORRECT — immediately after the line “The weather will turn cold” (line 5), the speaker returns to the current moment: “But that all happens later” (line 6). These lines help develop a central theme by emphasizing the speaker's choice to value and focus on the present moment. The “But” at the start of line 6 shows the speaker pulling back from the future and refocusing on the present, thus emphasizing the importance of savoring “the moment I am walking inside of” (line 22).

questions.question: Read lines 7-9 from the poem. “For now it is the early edge of fall, / leaves green still while the air narrows, / is slightly crisp,” The word choice in the lines helps convey the speaker's belief that

options.A: the beauty of the current season should still be appreciated.
options.B: the changes in the weather signify the end of the most pleasant season.
options.C: the transition from one season to another happens swiftly and without warning.
options.D: the change in the weather is so subtle that people rarely observe or feel it.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT — words and phrases in these lines, such as “leaves green still” and “slightly crisp,” have a positive connotation, indicating the speaker believes in appreciating this season while it still lasts. B. Incorrect — although imagery such as “leaves green still” and “slightly crisp” in these lines suggests the speaker enjoys the season, the speaker never indicates the present season is the most pleasant of all seasons. C. Incorrect — the phrases “the early edge of fall” and “the air narrows” in these lines imply the season is just beginning to change, but there is no indication from these phrases that the changes will be swift and without warning. In fact, the narrowing of the air could be a warning of a greater, more gradual change in weather. D. Incorrect — the speaker experiences the change in weather as subtle (“the air narrows, / is slightly crisp”), but the speaker does not refer to the viewpoints of others. The entire viewpoint in the poem is personal and introspective, as represented by the use of the pronoun “I” throughout.

questions.question: Which idea does the comparison of the brownstone houses to “a pop-up picture book I could have had as a child, / but didn't” in lines 20-21 convey?

options.A: It reveals that some people are still influenced by powerful images from childhood.
options.B: It indicates that the neighborhood the speaker is walking through is charming and appealing.
options.C: It suggests that the speaker has wanted to live in the neighborhood since childhood.
options.D: It suggests that people often experience lingering regret from their past.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — while the lines explain that the neighborhood reminds the speaker of images from childhood pop-up books, those images are not described as very powerful or influential. B. CORRECT — pop-up picture books are likely to delight a child with their unique, often beautiful representations of buildings that pop up out of the page. The comparison in these lines helps explain how the speaker views these brownstones with a childlike wonder and appreciation. C. Incorrect — though in these lines the speaker compares this neighborhood to scenes in children's pop-up picture books, there is no clear evidence the speaker wants to live there, only that the speaker appreciates its appeal. D. Incorrect — the lines state that the speaker did not have a “pop-up picture book” of the neighborhood's brownstones as a child, but not in a way that emphasizes regret. Rather, the speaker compares the neighborhood to images from pop-up books in general to suggest that the neighborhood looks whimsical/delightful.

questions.question: Read these lines from the poem. “I can already see how this will end.” (line 1) “How Brooklyn makes me nostalgic / for the moment I am walking inside of.” (lines 21-22) The lines develop a central idea of the poem by

options.A: suggesting the speaker's desire to find a way to break free from the repetitive pattern of daily life.
options.B: revealing the speaker's feelings of disappointment over the predictable change in season.
options.C: emphasizing the speaker's awareness of the future significance of the present moment in the setting.
options.D: showing the speaker's anticipation of specific emotions caused by an intimate knowledge of the setting.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — these lines suggest life is governed by repetitive patterns, such as the change of seasons, but do not suggest the speaker wishes to break free from these natural cycles; a desire for freedom is not a central idea of the poem. B. Incorrect — although the speaker acknowledges that colder weather will inevitably bring disappointment, the speaker does not suggest the predictability of changing weather is itself disappointing. Rather, the speaker recognizes the value of enjoying the present moment. C. CORRECT — these lines connect the present warmer weather with the future colder weather and develop the central idea that the present “moment I am walking inside of” must be embraced because the speaker will be “nostalgic” for it in the future. D. Incorrect — in these lines, the speaker is aware that specific emotions will occur in the future, during cold weather, but this awareness is only part of the more complex central idea of the poem, which is that current emotions and feelings must be recognized, experienced, and appreciated.

questions.question: The speaker's thoughts throughout the poem develop a theme by showing that

options.A: although people may hold expectations for the future, some people long for present experiences while they are still happening.
options.B: though people come from different places, most people feel drawn to the special charm a city holds.
options.C: although people can make decisions about their life, there will always be some things beyond their control.
options.D: though general expectations exist, people have no way of knowing what a given day will actually bring.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT — the speaker's thoughts develop some tension because seasonal change will inevitably come: “The weather will turn cold” (line 5). However, the speaker is still able to enjoy the present experience because “that all happens later” (line 6). In lines 21-22, the speaker begins to describe experiences that create a longing for the present, even while it is still happening (“How Brooklyn makes me nostalgic / for the moment I am walking inside of”), developing a theme of the poem. B. Incorrect — the speaker's thoughts reveal an appreciation for the city, but this appreciation is highly personal and individual; these thoughts do not indicate that most people will feel drawn to cities. C. Incorrect — some things, such as seasons, are beyond human control, as the speaker concedes: “I can already see how this will end” (line 1). However, the theme of the poem is not that certain things are inevitable, but that one can live in the present moment and enjoy that experience before change occurs. D. Incorrect — the speaker's thoughts are not showing that people are surprised by what the days bring; the thoughts of the speaker suggest that people experience many seasons in Brooklyn and have an opportunity to enjoy each one before it changes.

sentence_paragraphs.text: In 2004, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) landed a rover, or robotic vehicle, named Opportunity on the surface of Mars.
The rover’s mission was to search for evidence of water and life on the planet.
The rover was designed to gather data on Mars for about 90 days, but Opportunity’s assignment did not come to an end until nearly 15 years later in 2019.
During the rover’s mission, a high-resolution camera on the rover’s robotic arm took magnified photographs of the surface of Mars.
The photographs revealed small round rocks scattered across the surface of the planet.
The scientists nicknamed these rocks “blueberries” based on the rocks’ resemblance to the fruit.
These rocks were important because their spherical shape suggested that liquid water may have flowed over them for a substantial amount of time.
Opportunity continued to provide valuable data about craters and other surface features.
Throughout the mission, the rover traveled a total of 28.06 miles across Mars’ surface.
When Opportunity had traveled nearly the length of a marathon, scientists celebrated the accomplishment by naming the valley that the rover was in Marathon Valley.
However, in 2018, a dust storm spread all over the planet, putting the rover’s progress on hold.
Prior to this planet-wide dust storm, minor dust storms had periodically deposited a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover.
These prevented it from charging its batteries.
Scientists then had to rely on the passing winds and dust devils to clean off the solar panels.
After the massive 2018 dust storm subsided, scientists expected to be able to reestablish communication with Opportunity.
They made repeated attempts but to no avail.
In 2019, NASA finally declared Opportunity’s mission complete.
Opportunity was an important asset in scientists’ study of Mars; it returned valuable data about our neighbor planet and survived powerful dust storms.
NASA described the mission of Opportunity as “one of the most successful and enduring feats of interplanetary exploration.”
Even though this rover’s journey ended, other rovers still roam the surface of Mars.

questions.question: Which sentence should follow sentence 3 to **best** introduce the topic of the passage?

options.A: Despite the challenges of operating on the surface of another planet, the Opportunity rover made many valuable contributions to the field of space research.
options.B: The Opportunity rover mission was a success because it informed NASA scientists about how water might have existed on Mars.
options.C: Throughout the historic mission of the Opportunity rover, NASA scientists had to overcome challenges created by the flaws in the rover’s design.
options.D: The Opportunity rover mission surpassed the original timeline of the assignment and allowed scientists to collect additional data about the planet Mars.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the sentence that should follow sentence 3 to best introduce the topic of the passage.

A. CORRECT. This sentence best introduces the passage’s topic: the Opportunity rover had many accomplishments on its mission, despite numerous challenges. Some of those accomplishments include providing high-resolution photographs (paragraph 2), traveling long distances (paragraph 3), and providing data about craters and other surface features (paragraph 3).

B. Incorrect. Although paragraph 2 discusses how photographs taken by the rover showed rocks that may have been shaped by water, this idea alone is not the topic of the entire passage.

C. Incorrect. While this sentence incorporates ideas about difficulties the scientists encountered because of the Opportunity rover’s design (paragraph 4), the main topic of the passage is not the design flaws and obstacles scientists encountered throughout the mission. The passage primarily focuses on the achievements of the mission.

D. Incorrect. While it is true that the Opportunity rover mission lasted much longer than planned (sentence 3), this fact is a supporting detail of the passage, not the main topic of the passage; surpassing the original timeline is only one of the rover’s many achievements mentioned in the passage.

questions.question:
Sentence 7: “These rocks were important because their spherical shape suggested that liquid water may have flowed over them for a substantial amount of time.”

Sentence 8: “[blank] Opportunity continued to provide valuable data about craters and other surface features.”

Which word should be added to the beginning of sentence 8 to provide a better transition to the third paragraph (sentences 8–11)?

options.C: Meanwhile,

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the word that should be added to the beginning of sentence 8 to provide a better transition to the third paragraph (sentences 8–11).

“Overall,” is incorrect and should not be added. While sentence 8 is a more general statement than sentence 7, the word “Overall” would imply that all of the third paragraph features general information about the Opportunity rover. Instead, paragraphs 2 and 3 both describe specific accomplishments of the Opportunity rover (the discovery of possible water on Mars and the distance the rover traveled), so these paragraphs require a word between them that does not transition from the specific to the general.

“Furthermore,” is incorrect and should not be added. The word “Furthermore” would suggest that the author is making an argument in paragraph 2 that is further developed by the statement in sentence 8 and the rest of paragraph 3. Because this is not the case, the word “Furthermore” is not a suitable transition from one paragraph to the next.

“Meanwhile,” is correct and should be added. The word “Meanwhile” is an appropriate transition to add to the beginning of sentence 8, since the actions of the Opportunity rover in paragraph 2 (taking photographs) and in paragraph 3 (traveling long distances) happened at the same time and both served critical functions to the overall mission.

“Consequently,” is incorrect and should not be added. The word “Consequently” would create a cause-and-effect relationship that does not exist between the paragraphs. The passage gives no indication that the rover’s actions in the third paragraph (traveling a far distance) resulted from the actions in the second paragraph (taking photographs).

questions.question: Which revision of sentence 11 **best** maintains the formal style established in the passage?

options.A: However, in 2018, a dust storm covered the planet, bringing the rover’s progress to a standstill.
options.B: However, in 2018, a dust storm shrouded the planet, impermanently halting the rover’s progress.
options.C: However, in 2018, a dust storm enveloped the whole of the planet, arresting the rover’s progress for a time.
options.D: However, in 2018, a dust storm covered up the whole planet, which quickly brought a stop to the progress of the rover.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the revision of sentence 11 that best maintains the formal style established in the passage.

A. CORRECT. This sentence uses clear and formal writing throughout. The phrase “covered the planet” is accurate and formal without being overly poetic, and “standstill” is a precise word for putting something “on hold,” as expressed by the original sentence, while maintaining the formal style of the passage.

B. Incorrect. Although the sentence is formal in style, the word “shrouded” is overly poetic, and the phrase “impermanently halting” is too stilted and formal for the style and tone of the passage.

C. Incorrect. Although the sentence is formal in style, the words “enveloped” and “arresting” are overly poetic, especially when used in the same sentence, and the phrases “the whole of the planet” and “for a time” are needlessly wordy and imprecise, compared with the formal scientific language of the passage.

D. Incorrect. The phrases “covered up the whole planet” and “quickly brought a stop to the progress of the rover” are less formal and unnecessarily wordy, compared with the formal style established by the rest of the passage.

questions.question:
Read this sentence.

**One of Opportunity’s major contributions was finding possible evidence of the presence of water on Mars.**

Where should the sentence be added to the passage?

options.B: at the beginning of the second paragraph (before sentence 4)
options.C: at the end of the second paragraph (after sentence 7)

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks where the sentence should be added to the passage.

A. Incorrect. While sentence 2 refers to Opportunity’s mission to search for evidence of water, sentence 3 mentions the rover lasting much longer than anticipated. Placing the sentence between these two ideas, rather than at the start of the second paragraph, where it introduces the topic of the paragraph, would create a disjointed and confusing experience for the reader.

B. CORRECT. The sentence introduces the idea of finding possible evidence of water on Mars, which is the main topic of the second paragraph.

C. Incorrect. The sentence sets up the main idea of paragraph 2, which is the possibility of water on Mars. As a concluding sentence, it would be repetitive and confusing.

D. Incorrect. The sentence introduces the possibility of water on Mars, while sentences 8 and 9 discuss other surface features and the distance traveled by the rover. Adding the sentence here would create a disorganized paragraph.

questions.question: What is the **best** way to combine sentences 12 and 13?

options.A: Preventing the rover from charging its batteries, minor dust storms had periodically deposited a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover prior to this planet-wide dust storm.
options.B: Periodically depositing a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover prior to this planet-wide dust storm, minor dust storms had prevented it from charging its batteries.
options.C: Minor dust storms, prior to this planet-wide dust storm, prevented the rover from charging its batteries because they had periodically deposited a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover.
options.D: Prior to this planet-wide dust storm, minor dust storms had periodically deposited a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover, preventing it from charging its batteries.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the best way to combine sentences 12 and 13.

A. Incorrect. The phrase “this planet-wide dust storm” in the original sentence 12 makes a direct reference to sentence 11 and therefore acts as a transition that should be kept at the beginning. In this sentence, the transition phrase is placed at the end of the sentence, making the phrase confusing. In addition, the sentence is unnecessarily repetitive and wordy.

B. Incorrect. This combination unnecessarily turns sentence 12 into an overly long dependent clause, making the connection between “it” and its antecedent, “the rover,” unclear and distracting from the subject of the sentence, “minor dust storms.”

C. Incorrect. Not only does this combination move the reference to “this planet-wide dust storm” farther from sentence 11, but it is also unnecessarily wordy, adding “because” and repeating “the rover.”

D. CORRECT. This sentence efficiently and accurately adds sentence 13 to sentence 12 as a dependent clause by changing “These prevented” to “preventing,” while also retaining the meanings of the original sentences 12 and 13.

grammar_questions.question:
The Clearwater Children's Museum reopened after a yearlong renovation, the museum quickly became the most visited attraction in the county. Staff say they expect the museum to welcome nearly 500,000 visitors a year. The museum features more than 80 hands-on exhibits, including a giant bubble lab and a miniature grocery store. A touring exhibit on ancient Egypt, borrowed from a university collection, is also on display at the museum.

Which part of the paragraph contains an error in sentence structure?

Select the one error.

options.C: exhibits, including

solution.exhibit_text:
“The Clearwater Children's Museum reopened after a yearlong renovation” and “the museum quickly became the most visited attraction in the county” are both complete sentences, so joining them with only a comma at “renovation, the” is a comma splice.

**Why this sounds right:** The sentence is already moving briskly through one factual detail after another (renovation, reopening, popularity), so the comma blends right in as part of that same list-like rhythm instead of standing out as the seam between two separate complete sentences.

**The concept:** A comma splice happens when you join two complete sentences (each with its own subject and verb) using only a comma. Test it by splitting the sentence in two at the comma — if both halves could stand alone with a period, the comma isn't strong enough on its own. Fix it with a period, a semicolon, or a connecting word like "and"/"but"/"so."

**More examples of this mistake:**
- "The museum closes at five, we still had time to see the dinosaur exhibit." (Two complete sentences joined by only a comma — needs a period, a semicolon, or a word like "but.")
- "She finished her homework early, she decided to go for a walk." (Same problem — "she decided to go for a walk" is a full sentence on its own and needs more than a comma to attach it.)

base_question.stimulus: In September 2016 the National Museum of African American History and Culture opened as part of the Smithsonian <u>Institution, the</u> museum is already the Smithsonian’s third most popular site. Experts say that they expect this newest Smithsonian facility to welcome nearly 4 million visitors a <u>year. The</u> museum features more than 30,000 <u>objects, including</u> Muhammad Ali’s boxing gloves and a dress sewn by Rosa Parks. A commemorative copy of the Emancipation <u>Proclamation, written</u> in 1863 during the presidency of Abraham Lincoln, is also on display at the museum.
base_question.question:
Which part of the paragraph contains an error in sentence structure?

Select the one error.

options.C: objects, including

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which part of the paragraph contains an error in sentence structure.

Choice 1: “Institution, the” contains an error in sentence structure. The comma between these two words creates a type of run-on sentence known as a comma splice because both clauses—“In September 2016 the National Museum of African American History and Culture opened as part of the Smithsonian Institution” and “the museum is already the Smithsonian’s third most popular site”—are independent clauses, and must be separated with either a period or semicolon. If a comma is used to join the clauses together, a conjunction such as and would need to be added after the comma [converting the comma splice into a correct compound sentence].

Choice 2: “year. The” is correctly constructed, with independent clauses on both sides of the period (“Experts say that they expect this newest Smithsonian facility to welcome nearly 4 million visitors a year” and “The museum features more than 30,000 objects, including Muhammad Ali’s boxing gloves and a dress sewn by Rosa Parks”).

Choice 3: “objects, including” is correctly constructed. The sentence is correct as written with the nonrestrictive appositive phrase (“including Muhammad Ali’s boxing gloves and a dress sewn by Rosa Parks”) properly preceded by a comma.

Choice 4: “Proclamation, written” is correctly constructed. The sentence is correct, with the nonrestrictive clause (“written in 1863 during the presidency of Abraham Lincoln”) properly offset by a comma on either side.

grammar_questions.stimulus:
(1) Seismograph stations along the coast have been recording data since 1998.
(2) Seismograph stations allow researchers to track small shifts in the fault line.
grammar_questions.question:
Read these sentences.

What is the **best** way to combine the sentences to clarify the relationship between the ideas?

options.A: While seismograph stations along the coast have been recording data since 1998, researchers track small shifts in the fault line.
options.B: Although there have been seismograph stations along the coast since 1998, they have allowed researchers to track small shifts in the fault line.
options.C: Seismograph stations along the coast, which allow researchers to track small shifts in the fault line, have been recording data since 1998.
options.D: Seismograph stations have been recording data along the coast, but researchers have been tracking small shifts in the fault line since 1998.

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) nests the purpose of the stations — tracking small shifts in the fault line — in a nonrestrictive “which” clause, keeping the main point (that the stations have been recording data since 1998) as the main clause. “While,” “although,” and “but” all wrongly suggest contrast or coincidence instead of purpose.

**Why this sounds right:** “While,” “although,” and “but” are all common, natural-sounding connector words, so none of them raises a red flag on its own — but none of them actually fit, since there's no real contrast between the stations recording data and what that data is used for.

**The concept:** When combining several short sentences about one subject, there's usually one "main point" and the rest are supporting details. The strongest combination makes the main point the main clause and folds the other facts in as describing phrases or clauses, in whatever order makes the most logical sense. Watch out for answers that just string everything together with "and," since that treats every fact as equally important and loses the sense of what matters most.

**More examples of this mistake:**
- Weak: "The bakery opens at six. It sells fresh croissants. Many customers line up before it opens." Stronger: "Many customers line up before the bakery opens at six to buy its fresh croissants." (Folds the supporting details into one sentence built around the real main point.)
- Weak: "The lake freezes every winter. Skaters flock to it. The ice can get over a foot thick." Stronger: "Every winter, skaters flock to the lake as it freezes to over a foot thick." (Same fix — one main clause, details folded in.)

base_question.stimulus:
(1) Flyby missions near Jupiter have been happening since 1973.
(2) Flyby missions allow scientists to collect data about Jupiter and its moons.
base_question.question:
Read these sentences.

What is the **best** way to combine the sentences to clarify the relationship between the ideas?

options.A: While flyby missions near Jupiter have been happening since 1973, scientists collect data about the planet and its moons.
options.B: Although there have been flyby missions near Jupiter since 1973, they have allowed scientists to collect data about the planet and its moons.
options.C: Flyby missions near Jupiter, which allow scientists to collect data about the planet and its moons, have been happening since 1973.
options.D: Flyby missions have been happening near Jupiter, but scientists have been collecting data about the planet and its moons since 1973.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the best way to combine the sentences to clarify the relationship between the ideas.

A. Incorrect. Even though the two ideas from the original sentences are incorporated into the combined sentence, the use of the conjunction “while” in the first part of the sentence suggests that there is a simultaneous but unrelated relationship between the two ideas, which is incorrect.

B. Incorrect. The combined sentence incorporates the ideas from both sentences, but the conjunction “although” suggests that scientists were allowed to collect data even though there were flyby missions, which is an inaccurate way to express the relationship between the ideas.

C. CORRECT. This sentence is the best way to combine the sentences because it accurately reflects the relationship between the ideas by using the nonrestrictive clause “which allow scientists to collect data about the planet and its moons” to describe the purpose of the flyby missions. (Nonrestrictive clauses are adjective clauses that give additional information about a word or phrase. They sometimes begin with the relative pronoun “which” and are set off by commas.) The idea that the missions “have been happening since 1973” follows the nonrestrictive clause.

D. Incorrect. The combined sentence uses the conjunction “but” to connect the ideas in the two original sentences. This suggests an adverse relationship between ideas, which is an inaccurate way to connect the ideas expressed in the original sentences.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) On the morning of October 3, 2021, a water main break flooded three blocks of downtown Fairview.  (2) Trapping dozens of commuters in standstill traffic for over two hours, water gushed across Main Street and into nearby storefronts.  (3) Longtime residents were particularly unsettled because an almost identical rupture had occurred decades earlier—on the exact same stretch of pipe!  (4) The infamous Fairview Flood of 1986, which closed downtown for three days, also started on Main Street, an eerie coincidence to say the least.

Which sentence in the paragraph contains an error in construction and should be revised?

There is only one error in construction.

options.C: Sentence 3

solution.exhibit_text:
In sentence 2, “Trapping dozens of commuters in standstill traffic for over two hours” needs to be followed by whatever actually did the trapping — the water main break or the street closure it caused — not “water,” which doesn't trap commuters in traffic by itself.

**Why this sounds right:** “Water” sits exactly where grammar expects the modified noun to go, and water genuinely is part of the scene — so it's easy to read past the fact that water gushing doesn't itself trap commuters in traffic; the break and the resulting road closure do.

**The concept:** When a sentence opens with a describing phrase followed by a comma, whatever noun comes right after that comma is what the phrase is describing. If that noun can't logically do or experience what the phrase describes, the modifier is "dangling" — it has nothing correct to attach to. Fix it by moving the right noun right after the comma, or by rewriting the phrase so it fits the noun that's actually there.

**More examples of this mistake:**
- "After practicing for months, the piano recital finally arrived." (The recital didn't practice — should be "After practicing for months, Mia finally performed in the piano recital.")
- "Having forgotten her umbrella, the rain soaked through her jacket." (The rain didn't forget anything — should be "Having forgotten her umbrella, Priya got soaked in the rain.")

base_question.question:
Which sentence in the paragraph contains an error in construction and should be revised?

There is only one error in construction.
base_question.stimulus: (1) On the evening of July 13, 2019, a major power outage affected the Upper West Side of Manhattan in New York City.  (2) Leaving approximately 73,000 residents without electricity for three long hours, lights did not function, refrigerators did not stay cold, and air conditioners did not work.  (3) Longtime city residents were particularly confused because an eerily similar event had occurred years earlier—on the exact same day!  (4) The famous New York City Blackout of 1977, which lasted for 25 hours, also happened on July 13, an odd coincidence to say the least.

options.C: Sentence 3

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence in the paragraph contains an error in construction.

Sentence 1: Construction is correct. An introductory prepositional phrase is correctly punctuated in sentence 1 and describes when the power outage occurred. Similarly, the direct object, “the Upper West Side of Manhattan in New York City,” is presented clearly in terms of what area was “affected” by the power outage.

Sentence 2: Contains an error in construction. In sentence 2, the phrase “Leaving approximately 73,000 residents without electricity for three long hours” is a dangling modifier because it is not clearly modifying any word or words in the sentence. It actually further describes the “power outage” in sentence 1. In clear and correct construction, all modifiers should be in the same sentence as and near the words they describe in order to avoid confusion.

Sentence 3: Construction is correct. A dash is used appropriately in sentence 3 to show a break in thought and to introduce the phrase “on the exact same day.”

Sentence 4: Construction is correct. Two commas are used correctly in sentence 4 to set off the nonessential clause “which lasted for 25 hours” from the rest of the sentence. Similarly, one comma is used to set off the nonessential appositive “an odd coincidence to say the least.” Both of these elements are nonessential to the sentence’s overall meaning and are thus correctly separated from the sentence by the use of commas.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) Priya spent several days preparing her entry for the regional robotics competition.  (2) First she assembled the chassis and wiring for her robot, testing each connection twice before moving on.  (3) Then she programs the robot's navigation code to better handle the maze, and obstacles in the final course.  (4) Finally she ran the robot through practice trials in the garage many times, adjusting the sensors and calibration after each attempt.

How should the paragraph be revised?

options.A: Sentence 1: Change **spent** to **had spent**, AND insert a comma after **competition**.
options.B: Sentence 2: Change **assembled** to **assembles**, AND insert a comma after **wiring**.
options.C: Sentence 3: Change **programs** to **programmed**, AND delete the comma after **maze**.
options.D: Sentence 4: Change **ran** to **runs**, AND delete the comma after **times**.

solution.exhibit_text:
“Programs” should be “programmed” to match the past tense established by “spent,” “assembled,” and “ran.” The comma after “maze” must go because “the maze and obstacles” is a two-item list, which doesn't take a comma before “and.”

**Why this sounds right:** “Programs” sits in the middle of a longer, detail-heavy sentence, so it's easy to skim past since it still describes a real, concrete action; and the comma before “and obstacles” feels like a natural pause before one more item, even though “the maze and obstacles” is really just a simple two-item list that doesn't need one.

**The concept:** When a sentence or paragraph describes a sequence of actions that already happened, every verb in that sequence should stay in the same tense — usually all past tense. If most of the surrounding verbs are past tense but one verb suddenly switches to present tense (or the reverse) with no real reason for the shift, that's a tense-consistency error. Find the "majority" tense nearby and match the odd verb out to it.

**The concept:** A comma goes before "and" when it separates the last item in a list of three or more, or when "and" is joining two complete, independent sentences. But when "and" is just linking two verbs or phrases that share the same subject, no comma belongs before it — adding one wrongly suggests a third list item, or a second full sentence, that isn't actually there.

**More examples of this mistake:**
- "The chef chopped the vegetables, and seasoned the soup." (No comma needed — "and seasoned" shares the same subject, "the chef"; it isn't a second full sentence.)
- "The hikers reached the summit, and admired the view for an hour." (Same fix — delete the comma.)
- "She walked into the room, picks up her bag, and left." ("Picks" breaks the past-tense sequence — should be "picked.")
- "He studied all night, wakes up early, and aces the test." ("Wakes" and "aces" should be "woke" and "aced" to match the rest of the sequence.)

base_question.stimulus: (1) Danielle <u>spent</u> several hours preparing for an upcoming audition for a <u>play</u> at the community theater.  (2) First she <u>did</u> vocal exercises to practice her diction and <u>projection</u> so that her words would carry clearly throughout the large auditorium.  (3) Then she <u>studies</u> the text of the monologue to better understand the <u>emotions,</u> and motivations of the character she plans to portray.  (4) Finally she <u>recited</u> her monologue in front of a mirror many <u>times,</u> making slight adjustments and improvements to her performance each time.
base_question.question: How should the paragraph be revised?

options.A: Sentence 1: Change **spent** to **had spent**, AND insert a comma after **play**.
options.B: Sentence 2: Change **did** to **does**, AND insert a comma after **projection**.
options.C: Sentence 3: Change **studies** to **studied**, AND delete the comma after **emotions**.
options.D: Sentence 4: Change **recited** to **recites**, AND delete the comma after **times**.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks how the paragraph should be revised.

A. Incorrect. The revisions in this option introduce new errors. The word “spent” is correct in the simple past tense because it encompasses the actions described throughout the rest of the paragraph, all of which happened during those “several hours.” Additionally, adding a comma after the word “play” would be incorrect because it would unnecessarily separate the prepositional phrase “at the community theater” from the rest of the sentence.

B. Incorrect. The revisions in this option introduce new errors. The word “did” is correct as written in the past tense because the past tense is used throughout the paragraph. There is no comma needed after the word “projection” because “so” is functioning not as a conjunction but rather as part of the conjunction phrase “so that,” which does not take a comma.

C. CORRECT. Changing the word “studies” from the present tense to the past tense “studied” is necessary to match the past tense established in the paragraph (“spent,” “recited”). Additionally, the comma after the word “emotions” needs to be removed because the words “emotions and motivations” are part of a group (series) of two elements, and when there are only two elements in a series, a comma is not used.

D. Incorrect. The revisions in this option introduce new errors. The word “recited” is correct as written in the past tense because the past tense is used throughout the paragraph. Also, removing the comma after “times” is incorrect because the comma is needed in order to separate the modifying phrase “making slight adjustments and improvements to her performance each time” from the main clause.
